t.superagui national park@-25.4,-48.2:
You cannot ride into Superagui, and that is exactly why it is still here. The national park covers islands, mangroves, beaches and lowland Atlantic Forest on the northern coast of Paraná state in southern Brazil, and it belongs to the UNESCO-listed Atlantic Forest South-East Reserves. Access is by boat, mostly from Paranaguá or from the small town of Guaraqueçaba, and the reward is a stretch of coastline with no roads, few people and a very rare monkey: the black-faced lion tamarin, which scientists only described in 1990 and which lives in a tiny area of these forests.

So the ride is about getting to the edge. From Curitiba, the main highway drops steeply through the Serra do Mar toward the coast, but the far better choice for a rider is the Estrada da Graciosa, a historic road built in the nineteenth century that winds down the mountains through dense forest, much of it laid with old cobbles. It is narrow, twisty, often wet and slippery, with hydrangeas along the verges and lookout points over the green wall of the Serra. Take it slowly and enjoy it; it is one of the classic rides of southern Brazil.

At the bottom, Morretes is the place to eat barreado, a slow-cooked beef stew that is the regional dish, served with banana and manioc flour. Antonina, nearby, is a sleepy colonial port town, and Paranaguá, around thirty-seven kilometres from the park as the crow flies, is a busy port city with all the fuel, shops and services you could want. The road toward Guaraqueçaba is long, partly unpaved and can be muddy after rain, so check conditions before committing to it.

The Atlantic Forest is one of the most threatened forest systems on the planet, yet here it still runs unbroken from mountain to sea. Mangroves fringe the bays, dolphins swim in the estuary, and the air smells of salt, mud and flowering trees. Rain is frequent at any time of year, and summer brings heat, humidity and thunderstorms.

If you have time, park the bike in Paranaguá, take the boat across and spend a day walking the beaches of Superagui. If not, simply standing at the waterfront and looking across the bay at those dark green islands is enough to know you are at the edge of something rare.
t.ilha do mel ecological station@-25.5,-48:
No cars are allowed on Ilha do Mel, the honey island, at the mouth of the bay of Paranaguá in southern Brazil, and that is a large part of its charm. The island is a mix of sandy beaches, rocky headlands, mangroves and Atlantic forest, and most of it is protected as an ecological station and a state park. Its forests, beaches and mangroves are part of the Atlantic Forest South-East Reserves listed by UNESCO, a string of protected areas along the coast of Paraná and São Paulo that preserve some of the best remaining stretches of the Mata Atlântica. The number of visitors is limited, which keeps the island quiet even in summer.

The island has a small population living in fishing villages, such as Encantadas and Nova Brasília, connected by sandy paths. The Fortaleza de Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres, a Portuguese fortress from the eighteenth century, guards the entrance to the bay, and the lighthouse of Conchas, built in the nineteenth century on a hill, offers views over the island and the ocean. The Gruta das Encantadas, a sea cave, is the subject of legends about mermaids. Dolphins are often seen in the bay.

Your bike will have to stay on the mainland, but the approach is a treat. From Curitiba, the Estrada da Graciosa, a historic road built in the nineteenth century, descends the Serra do Mar through dense Atlantic forest, with cobbles, hairpins and viewpoints over the coastal plain. It is slow, beautiful and sometimes slippery when wet, so ride with care. The main highway, the BR-277, is faster. From Paranaguá or Pontal do Sul, boats cross to the island. Summer is hot and humid with heavy rain, while winter is mild.

Paranaguá has fuel and services, and Pontal do Paraná is the departure point for the shorter crossing, with secure parking for vehicles. On the island, there are simple restaurants and guesthouses, and the food is based on fish and seafood, with barreado, a slow-cooked beef stew from the coast of Paraná, as a regional speciality. Pack light, take the boat, and spend a day walking the beaches and forest trails; after the hairpins of the Graciosa, the silence of a car-free island is a gift.
t.zone state park pau oco turistical prese:
In 1873, the province of Paraná in southern Brazil opened a road down the Serra do Mar from Curitiba to the coast, and it is still there, paved with stone setts, winding through the Atlantic forest in more than a dozen kilometres of bends. The Serra do Mar here is part of the Atlantic Forest South-East Reserves, listed by UNESCO in 1999, one of the largest remaining stretches of a forest that once covered much of the Brazilian coast.

The Atlantic forest is extraordinarily rich, with towering trees, bromeliads, orchids, palms and tree ferns, and an abundance of birds, monkeys, frogs and insects. In the mountains, mist often hangs in the valleys, and waterfalls tumble down the slopes. The rainfall is heavy, and the forest is always green.

Riding the Graciosa is a pleasure, but the stone surface can be slippery when wet, which is often, and the road is narrow, with tight bends and steep gradients. Go slowly, enjoy the views, and stop at the viewpoints and rest areas along the way, some with kiosks selling snacks and drinks. On weekends, the road is popular with cars and motorcycles, so a weekday is better. At the bottom, the road reaches Morretes, a colonial town on a river, and Antonina, an old port on the bay of Paranaguá.

Morretes is famous for barreado, a traditional dish of beef slow-cooked for many hours in a sealed clay pot, served with cassava flour, rice and banana; it originated as a festival food that could cook for days. The Curitiba–Paranaguá railway, built in the 1880s through the mountains, is another engineering marvel, and the train journey down the Serra do Mar is a popular excursion.

Antonina, about twenty-four kilometres away, has fuel and basic services; Piraquara and Quatro Barras, closer to Curitiba, are larger, and Curitiba has everything. The weather in the Serra do Mar is changeable, with rain likely at any time of year, so bring rain gear. The best time to visit is from autumn to spring, when temperatures are milder; summers are hot and humid. Stop in Morretes for barreado and a glass of cachaça, then ride back up the Graciosa in the afternoon light.
t.pratapgad@17.9,73.6:
Pratapgad stands on a spur of the Sahyadri, the Western Ghats, about twenty kilometres from the hill station of Mahabaleshwar, guarding the old route between the Deccan plateau and the Konkan coast. Shivaji, founder of the Maratha state, had the fort built in the 1650s, and in 1659 it was the scene of the most famous episode of his life. Afzal Khan, a general of the Bijapur Sultanate, came with a large army to crush him, and the two met for a parley below the fort. Accounts differ on who struck first, but Shivaji, wearing armour under his clothes and the wagh nakh, a claw-shaped weapon, on his hand, killed Afzal Khan, and his troops hidden in the forest routed the Bijapuri army. The story is told across Maharashtra with immense pride, and Afzal Khan's tomb lies below the fort.

The fort has two parts, a lower fort with a temple to the goddess Bhavani, built by Shivaji, and an upper fort with a statue of him on horseback. The walls follow the edge of the cliffs, and the views over the forested valleys and ridges of the Ghats are spectacular. Monkeys wait at the steps for pilgrims' snacks; keep your bag closed.

The ride is the real reward. From Mahabaleshwar, the road drops through dense forest and then descends the Ambenali Ghat towards Poladpur and the coast, a long series of hairpins with drops over the Konkan below. The surface is variable, with potholes and gravel in places, and buses and trucks take the corners wide, so stay well left and use the horn at blind bends, as everyone else does.

The monsoon transforms everything. From June to September, the Western Ghats receive enormous rainfall, and Mahabaleshwar is one of the wettest places in India. Waterfalls pour from every cliff and the forest turns an electric green, but the roads become slippery, landslides happen, and visibility in the clouds can drop to a few metres. The months after the monsoon, October to February, are the best for riding, with cool mornings and clear skies.

Mahabaleshwar and Panchgani have fuel, hotels and restaurants; Mahad is the town on the coastal side. Mahabaleshwar is famous for its strawberries, grown on the plateau, and served with cream at roadside stalls in winter. Have a cup of sweet chai at the foot of the fort before the climb.
t.salto morato private reserve@-25.2,-48.3:
On the Paraná coast of Brazil the Atlantic Forest comes down almost to the sea, and Salto Morato is a private reserve that protects a good piece of it. A few thousand hectares of dense, wet forest, ferns, palms, orchids and giant trees covered in moss, with a trail that leads to a waterfall of about a hundred metres plunging down a green cliff. The Atlantic Forest was once enormous, running along most of the Brazilian coast, but today only a small fraction survives, and this area, with its neighbours in the Serra do Mar, is one of the best-preserved parts, recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage cluster.

The reserve was created by a Brazilian conservation foundation and has been a model for private protection, with trails, a research programme and guides from the local community. Wildlife is rich but shy: howler monkeys call at dawn, toucans and parrots cross the canopy, and jaguars and ocelots live in the forest, though you are very unlikely to see one. The nearby town of Guaraqueçaba and the bays of Paranaguá are fishing country, with mangroves, oyster beds and old Portuguese houses, and the pace of life is slow.

Riding here is an adventure. Approaching from Curitiba, the highway to Paranaguá descends the Serra do Mar in a long, spectacular series of bends through cloud and forest, with viaducts, tunnels and trucks that can slow progress. The final roads toward the reserve may be unpaved, and in the rain they become slippery and deep with mud, so check conditions locally and consider the season. The dry months from May to September are easier, but this is one of the wettest parts of Brazil, and showers can arrive at any time. Take rain gear and expect everything to feel damp.

Food near the reserve is simple, with fish, rice and beans, and fresh fruit juices. Visits usually need a fee and sometimes a guide, so check opening times in advance, and bring insect repellent and sturdy shoes for the trail, because a wet forest path is rarely dry.
t.pico do marumbi state park@-25.4,-48.9:
There are two ways down from Curitiba to the sea, and both are worth knowing. The modern highway, the BR-277, hurtles down the Serra do Mar in a series of viaducts and tunnels, and the old road, the Estrada da Graciosa, built in the nineteenth century, winds through the same forest on cobblestones, with bends so tight and views so green that bikers talk about it for years. The Serra do Mar is a steep coastal range, covered in Atlantic Forest, with clouds that cling to the peaks, and Pico do Marumbi, at about fifteen hundred metres, is the rocky summit that dominates the skyline.

The state park around it is a favourite of hikers, with trails to the summit that need a good day and a bit of scrambling, and a historic railway, the Serra Verde Express, which runs from Curitiba to Morretes through the forest on a line built in the 1880s. Morretes, at the foot of the mountains, is famous for barreado, a slow-cooked beef stew eaten with manioc flour and banana, which locals insist on serving in clay pots.

Piraquara and Quatro Barras are the towns on the Curitiba side, with about forty thousand and seventeen thousand people, and both have fuel and food. Curitiba itself, a clean, well-organised city with parks and a good bus system, has everything a rider needs. The ride along the Graciosa is short but slow, and the surface is rough and cobbled in places, slick with moss in the shade, with sharp bends and narrow sections, so it demands care, particularly on a loaded bike. The BR-277 is faster but heavy with lorries going to the port of Paranaguá, and fog can cut visibility to a few metres.

The weather here is changeable, with mist and drizzle even in summer, and rain can fall in any month, so carry waterproofs. The clearest weeks are in winter, from June to August, when cold fronts clear the air and the peaks appear sharp. Take a thermos of coffee, stop at a viewpoint and let the clouds clear.
t.chhatrapati shivaji terminus@18.9,72.8:
Mumbai's great railway terminus is a cathedral built for engines. It was designed by the English architect Frederick William Stevens and completed in the late 1880s as Victoria Terminus, named for the queen who was also Empress of India, and its mixture of Victorian Gothic and Indian motifs is one of the most flamboyant of the age. Domes, spires, pointed arches, carved peacocks and lions, stained glass and stone gargoyles give the whole building a theatrical quality. It was renamed in honour of the Maratha king Shivaji in the 1990s, and is now on the World Heritage list. Locals still call it VT.

The station is not a museum but a working organism. Hundreds of thousands of commuters pass through it daily, and the suburban trains, jam-packed and open-doored, are part of Mumbai's mythology. Outside, the pavements teem with hawkers, taxi drivers, tea sellers and pigeons, and the black-and-yellow cabs and red double-decker buses go by in a constant stream.

Riding in south Mumbai needs a particular state of mind. Traffic drives on the left, horns are constant, and lane discipline is a loose idea. Buses, taxis, autorickshaws and handcarts all move in different ways, so watch every gap and anticipate abrupt turns. At dawn on a Sunday the streets are almost calm, and a run along Marine Drive, the curved seafront promenade known as the Queen's Necklace, is one of the great city rides. The monsoon from June to September brings heavy rain, flooded streets and slippery tramlines and manhole covers, and the heat before it is thick and heavy.

The map shows Uran across the harbour as the nearest listed town, which is a reminder that Mumbai sits on an island city at the end of a peninsula, with the sea on three sides. Fuel is easy to find in the city, though petrol stations in the very south are fewer, and food is everywhere, from vada pav and cutting chai at street stalls to old Irani cafes. Park carefully, since the police can be strict, and take care with security of the bike in crowded streets.
t.khanderi fort@18.7,72.8:
Khanderi is a small island fort in the Arabian Sea, a short boat trip off the Konkan coast south of Mumbai. Shivaji built it in the late seventeenth century to challenge the Siddis, the Abyssinian-descended admirals of Janjira, who held the neighbouring island of Underi, and the two forts glared at each other across a narrow stretch of water for decades. The Marathas built Khanderi first, and the Siddis answered by fortifying Underi, and the sea between them saw skirmishes and cannon duels. Today Khanderi carries a lighthouse and the remains of walls and bastions, and its rocks are surrounded by fishing boats.

From the mainland you cannot ride to the fort; you need a boat, and the crossing is dependent on tides and weather. Boats do not run in the monsoon, so the visiting season is from October to May. The nearest mainland town in the data is Alibag, about nine kilometres away, a coastal town with a fort of its own, Kolaba, which stands on a rock in the sea and can be reached on foot at low tide.

The ride along this coast is a different thing from Mumbai's chaos. Roads run among coconut and betel palms, past salt pans and small fishing villages, and the sea appears and disappears between the trees. The road quality varies, with some good stretches of asphalt and others broken by monsoon damage, and traffic is mixed with buses, trucks and local scooters. The light is strong and the humidity high, especially before the rains. Watch for sand on the road near beaches and for stray dogs and cattle on the highway.

Alibag has fuel, shops, small hotels and plenty of food, with fish thalis and prawn curry the local pride. Many weekenders come down from Mumbai by ferry from the Gateway of India, which makes the beaches busy on weekends. If you can, ride in the week, in the early morning, and pack a spare layer for the sea breeze. Evening light on the fort walls from the shore is a good reason to linger.
t.suvarnadurg@17.8,73.1:
The Konkan coast of Maharashtra is a long green strip between the Sahyadri hills and the Arabian Sea, and every few kilometres a fort stands on a headland or an island. Suvarnadurg, the golden fort, rises from a rocky islet just off Harnai, a fishing port with a morning market that is one of the sights of the coast. The fort was strengthened in the seventeenth century by Shivaji, the founder of the Maratha state, as part of his drive to build a navy, and later it became the base of the admiral Kanhoji Angre, who ruled the sea here for decades and clashed with the British, Portuguese and Dutch. The walls are of black basalt, thick enough to withstand cannon fire, and they stand out against the green water.

Boats from the harbour at Harnai carry visitors across the short stretch of water to the fort. Inside, the ruins include a well, storehouses and old bastions, and the views over the harbour and the coast are fine. The tide and the swell decide whether boats can land, so check with the boatmen before you set out. The fishing fleet comes in early, and the auction on the quay, with baskets of pomfret, prawns and mackerel, is a lively scene.

The riding down the Konkan is gentle compared with the Himalaya, though not without its demands. The coastal roads wind through coconut groves, over little rivers on narrow bridges, and past small temples and villages. Surfaces vary from smooth to rough, and in the monsoon, from June to September, the rain is torrential and the roads can be slippery or flooded. Trucks and buses on the main highway are fast and heavy, so ride defensively. The coast to the south, towards Ratnagiri, is famous for Alphonso mangoes, which ripen in April and May and are sold at roadside stalls.

Harnai has seven thousand people and a few petrol stations, so fuel is simple. Dapoli, in the hills behind, is a cooler place for a night. Seafood restaurants along the road serve fish curry with rice, and the sol kadhi, a pink drink of coconut milk and kokum, is the local way to cool the palate.

The cooler months, from November to February, are the best for riding. April and May are hot and humid.
t.panhala fort@16.8,74.1:
Panhala is where one of the most famous escapes in Maratha history began. In 1660 Shivaji was besieged here by the forces of the Bijapur sultanate and slipped away on a rainy July night, heading for the fort of Vishalgad, while a loyal commander, Baji Prabhu Deshpande, held back the pursuers in a narrow pass and gave his life doing so. The story is told in every Maharashtrian school and the pass, Pavan Khind, is a place of pilgrimage. The fort that Shivaji escaped from is among the largest in the Deccan, a long ridge top surrounded by walls and bastions, with three great gateways and a wealth of ruined buildings.

Panhala dates in its present form from the late twelfth century, and it passed through the hands of the Yadavas, the Bahmanis, Bijapur and the Marathas. The queen Tarabai, who led the Maratha resistance against the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb after her husband Rajaram died, ruled from here for a time. Among the sights are the huge granaries, the Teen Darwaza gate and the Sajja Kothi, a pavilion where Shivaji's son Sambhaji was held under guard. The views from the walls over the Sahyadri hills and the valleys of the Warna are wonderful, especially after the monsoon, when everything is green.

The ride up from Kolhapur is short but dramatic, with a winding ghat road that climbs through forest and open grassland to the ridge. The curves are tight, the surface variable, and in the rainy season, from June to September, the mist is so thick that you can barely see the road. Landslides are possible in heavy rain. On a clear winter day the view from the top of the climb is superb, and the road is good fun on a light bike.

Kolhapur, a large city nearby, is the place for fuel and a proper meal. Kodoli, with seventeen thousand people, and the small town of Panhala itself are smaller options. The local food is famously spicy, with a red mutton curry, tambda rassa, served with a white one, and Kolhapuri chappals, hand-made leather sandals, are sold in the bazaars.

The Koyna Wildlife Sanctuary, on this ride, lies farther north in the same range, with dense forest, tigers and leopards. The cool, dry months from October to February are the best time for riding.
t.elephanta caves@19.0,72.9:
The boat leaves from the Gateway of India in Mumbai and takes about an hour to cross the harbour, passing warships, container ships and fishing boats, to a green island of rock and trees where, in the sixth century or thereabouts, a group of sculptors carved a temple into the hill. Elephanta Caves, as the Portuguese called them after a giant stone elephant they found near the landing, hold a collection of Hindu rock-cut temples dedicated to Shiva. The great cave contains huge carved panels, and the most famous is the Trimurti, a six-metre-high three-faced bust of Shiva as creator, preserver and destroyer. The sculptures were damaged by soldiers and time, but they still have an extraordinary force.

A climb of about a hundred and twenty steps leads from the pier to the caves, past stalls selling souvenirs and cold drinks. Monkeys live on the island and are happy to take food from tourists, so be careful. The caves are closed on Mondays, and the last boat back leaves in the afternoon, so check times in advance. The island was listed by UNESCO in 1987.

Riding to this place is a matter of getting to the harbour. Bikes cannot go on the ferry, so you leave yours at the Gateway of India, in a parking area, or at the mainland ports on the other side. The roads through Mumbai are crowded, noisy and fast, and a rider needs to be alert for buses, autorickshaws and pedestrians. The long sea bridge linking Mumbai with Navi Mumbai, the Atal Setu, does not allow two-wheelers, so the way to the Uran side is by the older roads along the harbour. The monsoon, between June and September, brings heavy rain and flooding, and the sea can be too rough for the ferry.

Uran, with twenty-five thousand people, has fuel and food, and the Navi Mumbai area has a big range of services. Raigad, on this ride, is the hill fort that was the capital of Shivaji's kingdom, farther south.

The best time to visit is between November and February, when the weather is cool and the sky is clear. Take water and sun protection, and wear shoes that grip on the steps.
t.vijaydurg@16.6,73.3:
Vijaydurg is a sea fort on the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, built on a rocky headland where the Vaghotan river runs into the Arabian Sea, and the setting alone is worth the ride. The fort was an old hill-fort of the Shilahara king Bhoja before Shivaji took it in the seventeenth century, rebuilt it, and made it one of the main bases of the Maratha navy. Later Kanhoji Angre, the admiral who held the coast against Portuguese, British and Dutch ships, used it as a harbour for his fleet, and the walls, bastions and triple line of defences look out over water that his ships once patrolled. They say there was an underwater wall to wreck enemy vessels that came too close, a story told at the gate with some pride.

The Konkan is one of India's loveliest coastal strips, with laterite plateaus, coconut and cashew groves, red-tiled villages and a string of quiet beaches between rocky points. Mango trees grow everywhere, and the Alphonso mangoes from nearby Devgad are the most prized in the country, picked in April and May and sold from roadside stalls. In the monsoon, from June to September, the whole region goes brilliant green but the rain is heavy enough to make riding miserable and landslides common, so go between October and February, when the air is warm and dry and the sea is calm. March and April get hot.

The ride along the coast road is slow and rewarding. Roads are narrow, patched and often one-and-a-half lanes wide, running up and down over laterite ridges and through small villages, with sharp bends, buses that take the middle and cows that take the rest. The surface is better on the main highway, NH66, which runs inland, but the coast roads have the views. Watch for loose gravel on corners and for sand blown across the tarmac near the beaches. Ferries across estuaries sometimes replace bridges, and timings should be checked locally.

Rajapur, twenty-odd kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town, with a population over ten thousand, and it is the place to count on for fuel and a mechanic. Smaller villages may have a pump, but they are not to be relied upon, so fill the tank in Rajapur or Devgad. Konkani cooking is built around fish, coconut and kokum, a sour fruit, and a thali of fried bombil, rice and sol kadhi, the pink kokum drink, is the right lunch after an hour on a hot road. Carry water and wear sun protection.
t.chilas@35.4,74.1:
Chilas is a hot, dry town on the upper Indus, where the Karakoram Highway runs through one of the most dramatic gorges on earth. Here three of the world's great mountain ranges, the Himalaya, the Karakoram and the Hindu Kush, meet within a few dozen kilometres, and the Indus carves a trench between them that is deeper than the Grand Canyon in places. The stony hillsides above the town are bare and brown, which makes the snowy bulk of Nanga Parbat, at 8,126 metres the ninth highest mountain in the world, seem even more unlikely when it appears over the ridge.

The town is also a trading and crossing point, and the hills around it are covered with petroglyphs. Thousands of carvings and inscriptions, in Sogdian, Kharoshthi, Brahmi and Chinese as well as other scripts, were left by travellers on the old Silk Road branch that ran through here, and many of them are Buddhist stupas, ibex and hunters pecked into dark rock faces by the river. The sites at Chilas and nearby Thalpan are the best known; many are being drowned or moved as dams rise upstream on the Indus.

For riders, Chilas is the gate to the Babusar Pass road, which climbs from the Indus up to the pass at about 4,170 metres and then drops into the green Kaghan valley toward Naran. The road is steep and in places rough, with hairpins, loose gravel, unfenced drops and sudden weather, and it is usually open only from early summer to autumn; snow can close it, and landslides can too. Check locally before you set out. The Karakoram Highway itself is a feat of engineering but is regularly cut by rockfalls and floods, and heavy trucks make the narrow sections slow.

Fuel is available in Chilas, which is the last reliable stop before the pass, and basic hotels and roadside restaurants serve lentils, chapati, grilled meat and strong sweet tea. Summer days are fierce, with temperatures over forty degrees in the gorge, while the pass above is cold even in July.

Start early, because afternoon wind and weather build, and give yourself time to drive the descent in daylight.
t.murghab@38.2,74.0:
Murghab is a town at the top of the world, or close to it. At around 3,600 metres on the high Pamir plateau in eastern Tajikistan, it is among the highest settlements in Central Asia, a scatter of low buildings and shipping containers set on a vast, cold desert of gravel, with bare mountains standing on every side. The air is thin and dry, the sky is an intense blue, and the nights can fall well below freezing even in summer. In winter, temperatures drop to minus thirty or lower.

The town is the commercial heart of the Eastern Pamirs, and its population is mostly Kyrgyz, descendants of herders who live in the highlands with yaks and sheep, so you will often see felt hats, yurts and women in bright scarves. The bazaar is a row of repurposed containers selling basics, and the guesthouses offer simple beds and warm food. Nearby, the plateau holds the Marco Polo sheep, the great-horned argali that the Venetian traveller described in his account, though they are difficult to see.

The Pamir Highway passes through here on its way from Khorog to Osh. East of Murghab the road climbs to the Ak-Baital pass, at about 4,655 metres the highest point on the highway, before dropping to Lake Karakul, a deep salt lake that fills a crater, at nearly 3,900 metres. The road surface varies, from good tarmac to broken stretches and washboard gravel, and the altitude takes its toll on both riders and machines. Fuel carburation changes and engines lose power, and headaches, nausea and sleeplessness are common. Take time to acclimatise, drink plenty of water and descend if symptoms become severe.

Murghab has fuel, though supply can be erratic and the quality uncertain, so carry a reserve, and ask at the guesthouses where to find petrol. Bring cash in Tajik somoni, since cards rarely work. Meals are simple, with bread, soup, noodles and strong tea.

Summer, from June to September, is the only reliable season, and even then, snow can fall any day.
t.hunza karimabad@36.3,74.7:
Karimabad is the main village of the Hunza valley, a green ribbon of terraced fields in the middle of some of the highest mountains in the world. The village sits on a hillside at about 2,500 metres in northern Pakistan, and from its terraces you look across to the great snow peaks of Rakaposhi, Ultar Sar and Lady Finger, rising to more than seven thousand metres. Apricot trees grow everywhere, and in spring their blossom fills the valley with white and pink, while in autumn the whole slope turns gold and red. The valley has long been a quiet world of its own.

Two forts stand above the village, Baltit and Altit, and they are the heart of its history. Baltit Fort, perched on a rock above the houses, is more than seven hundred years old in parts and was the seat of the Mir, the hereditary ruler of Hunza, until 1945. After restoration supported by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture, it now houses a museum with carved wooden rooms and a fine view of the valley. Altit, a little lower and older, is the original royal fort. Most people of Hunza are Ismaili Muslims, followers of the Aga Khan, and literacy and education levels are notably high compared with much of the region. Tales of exceptional longevity among Hunza people are popular but not well supported, so treat them as a story.

The Karakoram Highway runs through the valley, a road built by Pakistan and China between 1966 and 1979 at a heavy cost in lives, and it rewards the rider with endless views. The surface is generally paved, but landslides, rockfalls and washed-out sections are common, particularly in summer and after rain, and many bends are tight and blind. In 2010 a huge landslide dammed the river upstream at Attabad, creating a long turquoise lake that submerged part of the road, and traffic has since been rerouted through new tunnels. Check the current state of the road before travelling.

Fuel is available in Karimabad and Aliabad nearby, and hotels and guesthouses are plentiful, with views from the rooftops. Local dishes include walnut cake and apricot soup. Travel conditions are best from late spring to early autumn, and snow can block the road in winter. Rise early to see the first light on Rakaposhi.
t.passu@36.5,74.9:
Passu is a village at the foot of an immense rock wall, and the wall has a face that people photograph more than their own families. The jagged spires of the Passu Cones, also called Tupopdan, a ridge of dark granite and ice reaching about 6,100 metres, rise straight above the fields and the road in the upper Hunza valley, in a district called Gojal. A short distance away, the Passu Glacier flows down toward the river, its dirty grey tongue easy to reach on foot, and the glacier is a good example of how quickly the ice here moves and changes. In front of it, the valley floor is a patchwork of barley, potatoes and apricots in tiny stone-walled fields.

The most famous sight in the village is the Hussaini suspension bridge, a long and sagging footbridge of wooden planks and steel cables over the grey, fast river. It looks alarming, with large gaps between planks, and it is often described as one of the most dangerous bridges in the world, though local people use it with ease. Crossing is optional and at your own risk, and a section of a nearby bridge is in better condition. The mountains around the village hold many other peaks and glaciers, and trekking trails lead up to viewpoints and high pastures.

North of Passu the Karakoram Highway continues to Sost, the last town before the Chinese border, and then climbs to the Khunjerab Pass at about 4,700 metres, one of the highest paved border crossings in the world. The road here is demanding. It runs through narrow gorges and across gravel plains, with sections damaged by landslides, floods and glacial outwash, and the weather is cold and changeable. Altitude affects both rider and machine at the pass. The pass is open to travellers only at certain times and may require permits, so check conditions and rules well in advance.

Fuel is limited in this part of the valley, with the main supplies at Aliabad and Sost, so fill the tank when you can. Small guesthouses serve simple meals of bread, lentils and tea, and in the evening the temperature drops quickly. Autumn brings the best colour and clear air, though nights are cold.
t.khorog@37.5,71.6:
Khorog sits on the edge of Afghanistan, with only a river between them. The town lies at about 2,200 metres in the valley of the Gunt and Panj rivers, in the Gorno-Badakhshan region of Tajikistan, and from its streets you can see across the Panj to the villages and mountain tracks of the Afghan Pamir, close enough to hear the dogs. About thirty thousand people live here, the regional capital, and its character is calm and rather quiet, with tree-lined streets, Soviet-era buildings and a river promenade. A park beside the river is a pleasant place for a walk.

The people are mostly Pamiri, Ismaili Muslims who speak their own eastern Iranian languages, and their traditional houses, built around a central room with five pillars symbolising important figures in the faith, are a feature of the region. The Aga Khan Development Network has done a great deal here since the collapse of the Soviet Union, supporting a university campus, a hospital and the local economy. The Pamir Botanical Garden, at about 2,300 metres, is among the highest in the world and grows plants from across Central Asia. Apricots, mulberries and walnuts are sold in the market.

For riders, Khorog is a main stop on the Pamir Highway, one of the great high-altitude roads on earth. From here the road leads east and north across the high plateau, passing Ak-Baital Pass, at over 4,600 metres, and on to Murghab and Osh in Kyrgyzstan. A second road follows the Panj river southwest through the Wakhan corridor, with spectacular views of Afghan villages across the river. Surfaces vary from good tarmac to broken asphalt and gravel, and washouts and rockfalls are common. Altitude, cold and long distances between services make this a serious expedition, and you should prepare spares, tools and acclimatisation time.

Fuel is available in Khorog, but quality can be inconsistent, and farther along the highway stations are scattered, so carry spare fuel. Travellers need a permit for the Gorno-Badakhshan region, usually obtained with an e-visa, and security conditions should be checked before travel. The best season is from about May to October. Simple homestays offer bread, soup and tea, and the hospitality is very warm.
t.curitiba@-25.4,-49.3:
Curitiba is the city that other cities come to copy. Sitting on a cool plateau about nine hundred metres above the sea in southern Brazil, the capital of Paraná state became known in the 1970s for a handful of radical ideas: dedicated bus lanes with tube-shaped boarding stations, pedestrian streets, and a network of parks that took care of flood problems along the rivers. The result is a tidy, green and surprisingly calm city of nearly two million people, with a more European feel than most Brazilian places.

That European feel comes from the immigrants who settled the region in the nineteenth century: Poles, Ukrainians, Germans and Italians, who brought their churches, wooden houses and food. You can taste it in the cafes and markets, and see it at the Ukrainian memorial and the Polish forest on the edge of the city. The Botanical Garden, with its iron-and-glass greenhouse modelled on a Victorian conservatory, is a landmark, and the Oscar Niemeyer Museum, nicknamed the Eye because of its eye-shaped building, is a striking example of modern Brazilian architecture. Local food includes barreado, a slow-cooked meat stew, and chimarrão, the bitter maté tea sipped from a gourd.

For a motorcyclist, Curitiba is the gateway to one of the best rides in southern Brazil, the descent of the Serra do Mar to the coast. The old Graciosa road, a cobbled route built in the nineteenth century, drops through thick Atlantic rainforest, shrouded in cloud, with tight bends and dizzying views, though the cobbles are slippery when wet and a light, steady pace is wise. The newer BR-277 highway is faster and smoother, descending to the port of Paranaguá, and a mountain railway nearby, one of the most spectacular in the country, runs down to Morretes. Rain, mist and sudden changes in temperature are normal here, so pack waterproofs. The summer months are warm and wet, and winter can be cold, even with frost on the high ground.

There is no problem with fuel in the city, where stations are everywhere and many sell both petrol and ethanol. Keep documents handy, because police checkpoints are not unusual, and take care with bikes in city centres, where theft can be a problem. Park in guarded areas. The cafes of the old centre, around Largo da Ordem, make a fine place to rest.
t.mumbai@19.1,72.9:
Mumbai is a city that never quite stands still, and for a rider the first lesson is that the road belongs to everyone. Taxis, buses, rickshaws, scooters, handcarts, cows and pedestrians share every lane, and the horn is a language, used for greeting, warning and complaint. More than twelve million people live in the city proper, and many more in the surrounding region, making it one of the largest urban areas on earth. It was called Bombay until 1995.

The city grew from seven islands on the west coast of India, which were joined by land reclamation, and it became a great port under the British. The colonial buildings near the harbour, among them the Gateway of India, a basalt arch built to welcome a king, and the Victorian Gothic railway terminus, now a World Heritage site, still dominate the old south. The film industry, Bollywood, grew up in the north, and the beaches and the seafront promenade along Marine Drive fill each evening with people watching the sunset.

The ride that begins here follows the Konkan coast, a long strip of green land between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea, to the south. The road leaves the city through Navi Mumbai and Panvel, and the first hours are slow, with trucks and traffic, before it opens into hills, rice fields and coconut palms. Fuel is easy to find in the city and along the highway, though stations get sparser in the lush south. Avoid the monsoon months, from June to September, when rain is torrential and landslides can close the roads.

The coast is famed for its seafood, its fine mangoes and its quiet beaches. The Alphonso, a small golden mango from this region, is among the best in the world, and in April and May it is sold from roadside stalls. Leave before dawn to beat the traffic, and carry water. The road south becomes a pleasure, but the city has to be crossed first.
t.goa@15.3,74.1:
Goa is known for its beaches, but this part of it is something quite different. Near Sanvordem, in the south of the state, the land rises into the forested foothills of the Western Ghats, and the landscape is a mix of red laterite earth, cashew plantations, areca palms and small rivers. The area has long been associated with iron-ore mining, which left terraced hillsides and rust-coloured roads, and the town of Sanvordem still carries the character of a working place.

Goa was a Portuguese colony from 1510 to 1961, and the Portuguese influence is visible in the churches, the architecture, the food and even the names of the people. In Old Goa, not far to the west, the great Basilica of Bom Jesus holds the relics of St Francis Xavier, and the nearby Se Cathedral is one of the largest churches in Asia. Inland, the spice plantations around Ponda offer shaded walks among pepper vines, cardamom and vanilla, and a lunch served on banana leaves.

The roads inland are quieter than the beach routes, with long, winding stretches through jungle and farmland. Surfaces are mixed, with smooth tarmac in places and potholes in others, and monsoon rains from June to September can wash out stretches or leave them slick with mud. Trucks carry ore and goods along the main roads, and cows wander freely, so stay alert. Fuel is available in Sanvordem and other towns of a few thousand people, and the road north toward Sindhudurg passes small stations at regular intervals.

Food in Goa is distinctive, with fish curry and rice, pork sausages and vindaloo, and a sweet, layered cake called bebinca. Cashew feni, a strong spirit distilled from the fruit, is the local drink, and a small glass is enough. The best season is from November to February, when the air is dry and the sky clear.
t.ratnagiri@17.0,73.3:
Ratnagiri is a port town on the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, with a population of about seventy-six thousand, a lighthouse, a fort and a long strip of black-sand beach. The coast here is red laterite hills falling to the Arabian Sea, with coconut palms, cashew trees and mango groves along the roads, and the whole place feels green and slightly sleepy. It is the starting point for the ride south toward Goa.

The town is best known for the Alphonso mango, which is widely grown in the area and sold across India in spring. If your ride falls in April or May, buy a few from a roadside stall. Ratnagiri is also where the nationalist leader Bal Gangadhar Tilak was born, and where the last king of Burma, Thibaw, was kept in exile after the British deposed him in 1885. His former residence is a short walk from the centre. Ratnadurg, a fort on a headland, and the Bhatye beach with its lighthouse are good places for a view of the sea and sunset.

For the rider, the coastal road is a mixture of newly laid highway, older winding roads through villages and hilly stretches with sudden sharp bends. Winter, from November to February, is the best season, with clear skies and moderate temperatures.

Ratnagiri has fuel, ATMs, hotels and restaurants, and it is the largest town for a long stretch, so fill up here. Seafood is the local pride, particularly fried fish, prawn curry and the sweet-sour kokum drink that cools you down in the humid heat. Ganpatipule, a temple town with a beautiful beach, lies a short ride north.

Watch for cattle, trucks and sudden speed bumps in villages, and be ready for some heat and humidity in the afternoon. Starting early is the best way to enjoy the coast.
t.kalaikhum@38.5,70.8:
Kalaikhum lies in the deep, hot gorge of the Panj river in south-western Tajikistan, where the Pamir Highway's western arm runs along the border with Afghanistan. At about twelve hundred metres, it is low by Pamir standards, and the valley floor is dusty, warm and full of apricot trees. The river is the frontier: on the far bank lie Afghan villages of mud-brick houses and terraced fields, linked by narrow donkey tracks cut into the cliffs, and a rider can watch the daily routines of people walking, ploughing and herding only a few hundred metres away across the water.

The town sits where the Vanj and Panj rivers meet, in the Darvaz region, and old fort walls still stand on the hill. It is a modest place with a bazaar, a few guesthouses and a petrol station or two. Travellers on the highway use it as a stopping point on the long haul between Dushanbe and Khorog, and a meal of plov, rice with carrots and lamb, and green tea in a chaikhana is the standard welcome.

The riding is some of the most dramatic you can find. The road between Kalaikhum and Khorog hugs the river, cut into the rock face above the water, with sheer drops, tunnels, rockfalls and sections where the surface has been washed away by streams. In places it is paved, in others rough gravel and sand, with potholes that can swallow a wheel. Landslides can close it for hours after rain, and heavy lorries from China and Afghanistan struggle on the narrow bends. Ride slowly and stay away from the edge. It is not a place for a hurried rider.

Fuel is available in town but not everywhere beyond, so fill the tank and carry spare. Entry into this part of Tajikistan, the Gorno-Badakhshan region, requires a special permit that is handled through the e-visa system, and you should check the current rules before travelling. Summers are very hot in the gorge, so start early, and in spring the river runs brown and loud with meltwater. The peaks rise white on the horizon, and the glimpses of high snow above the heat are unforgettable.
t.khargush pass@37.5,73.2:
Khargush Pass, at 4,344 metres, is the high point of the road along the Wakhan corridor, and it feels like the roof of the world. The track climbs from the Panj valley near Langar, where the river runs along the Afghan border below the white wall of the Hindu Kush, up into a stony plateau of the eastern Pamirs, cold, windy and almost without people. From the top, you can see the snow-capped Hindu Kush to the south, the barren Pamir ranges to the north and an enormous, empty sky.

The road is a challenge. It is an unpaved track of rough gravel, sand and rock, with river crossings, steep grades and sections of loose scree, and it requires a bike with good ground clearance, good tyres and a rider who is not alone. Altitude brings its own problems, since the air is thin and the engine loses power, while the rider can suffer headaches and nausea. Weather can change fast, with snow possible even in summer, and the cold at night is severe. It is a place for experienced adventure riders with proper preparation.

The surroundings are remote but alive. On the high plateau, herds of yaks and sheep graze near summer camps, and the Kyrgyz herders who live in yurts offer tea and bread to passers-by. Lake Zorkul, the source of the Panj river and a protected nature reserve, lies a short distance to the south, and the high grasslands around it are the habitat of the Marco Polo sheep, a magnificent wild sheep with great spiralling horns, named for the Venetian traveller who described it in the thirteenth century. You may see marmots as well.

Murghab, a small town of containers and low houses at 3,600 metres, has a bazaar, a few guesthouses and basic supplies. Bring water, food, tools and spare parts, and tell someone where you are going, since phone signal is almost non-existent. A special permit is needed for the region, so check conditions before you go. The dawn light on the peaks is a reward for the cold.
t.urubici@-28.0,-49.6:
Frost on the grass in a country famous for beaches is the first surprise of Urubici. The town lies on the high plateau of the Serra Catarinense in Santa Catarina, at roughly 900 metres, and it is regularly named as one of the coldest places in Brazil, where winter mornings bring ice on puddles and, once in a while, a dusting of snow that makes the national news. The land is a patchwork of apple orchards, pine woods, pasture and araucaria trees, the monkey-puzzle conifers whose seeds, the pinhão, are boiled and eaten in winter.

The big reason to ride here is the Serra do Corvo Branco, a mountain road that slices through the escarpment between the plateau and the lowlands. At one point it passes through a cut in the rock with walls rising nearly a hundred metres on either side, so narrow and sheer that it feels like a canyon rather than a road. Tight turns, steep gradients and fog make it demanding, surface conditions have varied over the years, and it can be slippery when wet, so check the state of the road and go slowly, with your lights on. Up top, the views over the plateau drop away into green valleys and distant sea haze.

The area has other treats. The Morro da Igreja, a high headland topped with a weather station, has a rock arch, the Pedra Furada, where you can see the Serra do Rio do Rastro snaking down below, and several waterfalls such as the Véu de Noiva tumble from the cliffs near town. The cold weather also brings cosy cafés with hot chocolate, local cheese and honey, and wood fires in the evenings.

Plan the ride for midday in winter, when it is warmest, and the early morning in summer, before cloud builds. Urubici is a small town with fuel and basic services, and bigger towns such as Lages lie some way off, so start with a full tank if you plan to explore the backroads. Evenings are chilly all year, and bringing a warm layer and waterproofs is wise. Sunsets over the plateau, with the frost-white pastures turning pink, are one of the nicest rewards.
t.morretes@-25.5,-48.8:
Morretes is a small, quiet colonial town on the Nhundiaquara river, in the shadow of the Serra do Mar, and the way you get there is the best part of the visit. The Estrada da Graciosa, built in the nineteenth century to link the coast with the plateau around Curitiba, climbs and falls through the Atlantic forest in a series of cobbled and paved stretches, with hairpins, narrow bridges and views that open suddenly over the green slopes. Moss, ferns and bromeliads cover the trees, and the air is damp and rich with the smell of leaf litter.

The road is not for speed. Long sections are paved with old stones, which become treacherous when wet, and mist and rain are common in this part of Paraná, so ride slowly and keep your distance from other vehicles. Occasionally the road closes after storms or landslides, and in some areas there are restrictions on traffic and speed to protect the park, so check before you set out. When it is dry and clear, it is wonderfully peaceful, with birdsong and the sound of streams.

Morretes itself is famous for barreado, a dish of beef cooked for around twelve hours in a sealed clay pot with spices until it falls apart, then served with manioc flour, rice and banana. The tradition comes from the area's colonial past, and restaurants along the riverside serve it for lunch. There is also the cachaça and banana sweet made in the region. Walk across the old bridge, look at the colourful houses along the water, and sit by the river with a coffee.

The tourist train from Curitiba to Morretes follows a spectacular line down the same mountain, passing bridges and tunnels, and can be fun to watch as it passes. Antonina, thirteen kilometres away with about sixteen thousand people, sits on the bay and is also worth a stop for its old buildings, and it is the better place to find fuel, though Morretes itself has services. Piraquara and Quatro Barras are on the plateau side, where bigger towns offer repairs and supplies. Give yourself an easy afternoon and avoid the road at night.
t.lohagad@18.7,73.5:
In the monsoon, Lohagad disappears into the clouds and reappears, drenched and green, with waterfalls pouring off every ledge. This hill fort stands on a ridge of the Western Ghats a short distance from Lonavla, between Mumbai and Pune, and its walls and gateways crown a basalt plateau a few hundred metres above the surrounding valleys. Its name means iron fort, and it is one of the forts associated with the Maratha ruler Chhatrapati Shivaji, which in 2025 were grouped together on the UNESCO list as the Maratha Military Landscapes.

The fort has a long history, changing hands between the Marathas and the Mughals more than once in the seventeenth century. Climbing through its four great gates, each set higher than the last, you can see how hard it would have been to take by force. On the western side the ridge runs out into a narrow spur called Vinchu Kata, the scorpion's tail, with sheer drops on both sides. Nearby, the Buddhist rock-cut caves at Bhaja and Karla, carved around two thousand years ago, are well worth a stop for their pillared halls and stupas.

Getting there is a ride through Maharashtra's hills. The old Mumbai–Pune highway climbs through the Khandala ghat in a series of bends, with trucks, buses and monkeys sharing the road; note that two-wheelers are not allowed on the Mumbai–Pune Expressway. From Lonavla, a narrow road leads to the village of Lohagadwadi at the foot of the fort, from where you climb on foot, up steps that are slippery in the rains. The monsoon months of June to September are glorious but wet and crowded at weekends, and the cooler, drier months from November to February are the most comfortable.

Lonavla has plenty of fuel, food and accommodation, and it is famous for chikki, a crunchy sweet of jaggery and peanuts, sold in countless shops. Stalls at the base of the fort serve hot tea, vada pav and pakoras, perfect after a soaking climb. Carry water, watch your step on the wet stone and keep a careful eye on bags and snacks, because the monkeys here are bold and quick.
t.ilha do cardoso state park@-25.1,-48.0:
The southern tip of São Paulo's coast frays into a maze of islands, channels and mangroves, and the largest of the islands, Ilha do Cardoso, rises from the sea as a forested mountain ridge. It has been a state park since the 1960s, protecting a remarkable range of habitats in a small space: mountain rainforest, restinga scrub on sandy soils, mangroves, dunes and long empty beaches facing the Atlantic. It is part of the Atlantic Forest Southeast reserves listed by UNESCO.

There are no roads on the island and no cars, so the only way to get there is by boat, usually from Cananéia, a fishing town on the mainland side of the estuary. Cananéia claims to be one of the oldest settlements in Brazil, founded by Portuguese and Spanish sailors in the early sixteenth century, and its colonial streets and waterfront have a sleepy, salty charm. The waters around are known for oyster farming, and dolphins are often seen in the channels. On the island, small communities of traditional fishermen, known as caiçaras, live in villages along the shore and welcome visitors.

The ride to Cananéia from the BR-116 is a pleasant one, through the lowlands of the Vale do Ribeira, past banana plantations, small towns and river crossings, with long straight stretches and some gentle curves. Traffic is light, but road conditions vary, and summer rains can bring flooding and potholes. From Ilha Comprida, a long barrier island linked by bridge, you can ride along the coast with the sea on one side and the forest on the other.

Fuel and food are available in Cananéia, where restaurants serve fresh oysters, grilled fish and seafood stews. The boat trip to Ilha do Cardoso takes around an hour and runs according to tides and weather, so check schedules in advance. On the island, there are simple guesthouses and campsites, and you can hike trails through the forest to waterfalls and lookout points. Bring insect repellent, sun protection and plenty of water, and leave your bike securely parked on the mainland.
On the coast of Paraná, between the port city of Paranaguá and the beaches of Pontal do Paraná, the Guaraguaçu Ecological Station protects a stretch of lowland forest, mangrove and sandy restinga along the Guaraguaçu river. It belongs to the network of Atlantic Forest reserves that UNESCO lists for the south and southeast of Brazil, here around the Paranaguá bay, one of the best preserved estuaries on the Brazilian coast. Access to the station itself is restricted, as ecological stations are mainly for research, but the surrounding landscape gives a strong sense of what it protects.

The bay is a world of green and grey: mangroves lining muddy shores, forested islands such as Ilha do Mel, the dark mountains of the Serra do Mar rising behind, often wrapped in cloud. Birds are everywhere, including herons, egrets and the scarlet ibis, which has been seen again on this coast in recent years. Paranaguá, one of Brazil's largest ports for grain exports, has a historic centre with colonial buildings, while Antonina, at the head of the bay, is a quieter colonial town that feels stuck in time.

For riders, the jewel of the region is the Estrada da Graciosa, an old road from the plateau near Curitiba down the Serra do Mar to Antonina and Morretes. Much of it is paved with cobblestones and lined with hydrangeas and dense forest, with viewpoints and picnic spots along the way, and it can be very slippery when wet, which is often. The BR-277 offers a faster alternative between Curitiba and Paranaguá, busy with trucks heading to the port. Along the coast, roads to Pontal do Paraná are mostly flat and straight, heavily used in the summer holidays.

Fuel is easy to find in Pontal do Paraná, Paranaguá and Antonina. The local speciality is barreado, a slow-cooked beef stew traditionally prepared in a clay pot sealed with a paste of flour and water, served with manioc flour and banana, and Morretes is the place to try it. The climate is humid, with frequent rain, so pack waterproofs and enjoy the green that comes with it.
t.guaraquecaba ecological station@-25.3,-4:
Guaraqueçaba is one of those places in Brazil where the road gives up before the forest does. It lies on the northern shore of the great bay of Paranaguá, on the coast of Paraná state, surrounded by mangroves, islands, tidal channels and the steep, forested slopes of the Serra do Mar. The ecological station protects a large area of mangroves and coastal forest, and it is part of the Atlantic Forest South-East Reserves, a World Heritage Site that preserves some of the best remaining stretches of the Mata Atlântica, a forest that once covered much of Brazil's coast and has now been reduced to a fraction of its former extent.

The wildlife is extraordinary. The region is the stronghold of the red-tailed amazon, a parrot with a purple face that roosts on the islands of the bay, and the black-faced lion tamarin, a small primate found nowhere else. Dolphins swim in the bay, and the mangroves are full of crabs, herons and other birds. Fishing communities live on the islands and along the shore, much as they have for generations, with canoes, nets and small farms.

Getting here by bike is an adventure. The road from Antonina to Guaraqueçaba is largely unpaved, a long stretch of gravel and dirt through forest and farmland, with mud, ruts and river crossings after heavy rain. It is best ridden on a dual sport bike, in dry weather, with plenty of time. Many visitors arrive by boat instead, from Paranaguá, a trip of a couple of hours across the bay. The ecological station itself is a protected area with restricted access, so check with the authorities before planning a visit.

For tarmac riders, the region offers one of the classic roads of southern Brazil: the Estrada da Graciosa, a historic road paved with stones that winds down the Serra do Mar from near Curitiba to Morretes, through dense forest, with hairpins, waterfalls and viewpoints. Morretes is famous for barreado, a slow-cooked beef stew traditionally sealed in a clay pot. Antonina, a colonial port town, and Paranaguá, the main port of the state, have fuel and services. The climate is hot and humid, with heavy rain at any time of year, so pack accordingly.
t.raigad@18.2,73.4:
Raigad is a flat-topped mountain in the Sahyadri, the Western Ghats of Maharashtra, with cliffs falling away on almost every side, and it was chosen by Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj as the capital of the Maratha kingdom. In 1674 he was crowned here, a ceremony that announced the Marathas as a sovereign power in the face of the Mughal empire, and the fort became the political heart of the young state. Today the summit holds the ruins of the palace, the market street with its rows of stone shop plinths, water tanks cut into the rock, and Shivaji's samadhi, which draws a steady stream of visitors who come as pilgrims rather than tourists.

Getting to the top is part of the experience. There are a great many stone steps for those who walk, and a ropeway for those who would rather not, swinging up over the cliffs with the valley dropping away below. At the base, at Pachad, are the remains of the palace associated with Jijabai, Shivaji's mother. The views from the summit across the folded green ridges of the Konkan, especially after the monsoon, are spectacular.

Riding here is all about the season. The monsoon, roughly June to September, transforms the Sahyadri into an impossibly green landscape full of waterfalls, and it also makes the ghat roads slippery, foggy and prone to landslides; many local riders love it, but it demands care. October to February is the comfortable time, with clear skies and cooler air. The approach from the coast is via the Mumbai to Goa highway through Mahad, and from Pune you can come down one of the ghats, such as Varandha or Tamhini, which drop from the Deccan plateau to the coastal plain in long sequences of hairpins and views. Expect trucks, buses, people and animals on the road at all times.

Mahad, about seventeen kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel, food and mechanics; it has historical weight of its own as the place where B. R. Ambedkar led the Mahad Satyagraha in 1927 for access to public water. Around the base of Raigad you will find simple stalls selling tea, vada pav and kokum sherbet, a sour pink drink that is perfect in the heat. Start the climb early, before the sun gets high, and carry water.
t.rajgad@18.2,73.7:
In the folded hills of the Sahyadri, south-west of Pune, a great flat-topped mountain rises above the valleys with sheer cliffs on all sides and walls running along its crest. This is Rajgad, the king's fort, and for about twenty-five years in the seventeenth century it was the capital of Shivaji, the Maratha warrior king who carved out an independent kingdom against the Mughal Empire and the sultanates of the Deccan. It is one of the most revered places in Maharashtra, and climbing it is something of a pilgrimage.

The fort is spread across three spurs, called machis, Padmavati, Suvela and Sanjivani, each fortified with walls, bastions and gates, and a central citadel, the Balle Killa, at the top. Shivaji's son Rajaram was born here, and his first wife Saibai died here. The climb takes a few hours on foot, along steep paths with some rock steps and ladders, and the views from the top over the Sahyadri, with the forts of Torna and Sinhagad visible on neighbouring peaks, are enormous. Many people camp overnight at the fort to see the sunrise.

The riding to get here is excellent. From Pune, the road south along the old Pune-Satara highway, now NH48, is busy, but turning off towards Nasrapur and the villages below Rajgad, the roads become narrow and winding, climbing through the hills with tight bends and steep gradients. The surfaces are often rough, with potholes and gravel, and during the monsoon, from June to September, the hills turn emerald green, waterfalls pour from the cliffs, and the roads can be slippery and muddy. The monsoon is beautiful but challenging; the cooler winter months are more comfortable.

The Sahyadri, or Western Ghats, have clusters on the World Heritage list for their biodiversity, and the range is full of forests, grasslands and rivers home to many endemic species. On the plateaus, the monsoon brings a burst of wildflowers. Leopards, wild boar and birds such as hornbills live in the forests, though you are unlikely to see the shy ones.

Bhor, about twenty kilometres away, has fuel, shops and food. Nasrapur and the villages below the fort have small eateries serving Maharashtrian food like misal pav, a spicy curry with bread, and pithla bhakri, a simple chickpea flour dish with millet bread. Carry water and snacks for the climb, and wear proper shoes.
t.serra da graciosa turistical preservatio:
The Serra da Graciosa is the steep green escarpment that separates the high plateau around Curitiba from the coastal plain of Paraná, and the old Graciosa road that runs down it is among the most scenic in southern Brazil. The road was opened in the nineteenth century, linking the interior with the port of Antonina on the Atlantic coast, and for a long time it was the main way for mule trains carrying mate and goods down to the sea. It is about thirty kilometres long, and parts of it are still paved with old stone, which gives it a rattling, slippery character in the wet.

The surrounding forest is the Mata Atlântica, the Atlantic rainforest, which once covered the whole Brazilian coast and has been reduced to a fraction of its former size. In the Serra do Mar the forest remains thick and damp, with bromeliads, tree ferns, orchids and giant trees, and the mist clings to the slopes for much of the year. Waterfalls and rivers cut through the forest, and the bird life is rich, with toucans, tanagers and many species found nowhere else. The jagged peaks of the Marumbi range, which attract hikers, rise to the south, among them Olimpo, at over fifteen hundred metres.

The road is part of a protected landscape, and its treasures include the stone bridges, viewpoints and a few small restaurants and waterfall parks along the way. The descent is a long run of bends, with the forest closing in on both sides, and the temperature changes as you drop from the cool plateau to the warm, humid coast. Be careful: the wet cobbles and moss make for poor grip, fog can drop in suddenly, and the road is sometimes closed after landslides or heavy rain. Weekends bring cyclists and families, so ride gently.

At the bottom lies Morretes, a charming old town on the Nhundiaquara river, and the home of barreado, a stew of beef cooked slowly for many hours in a clay pot and eaten with manioc flour and bananas. The scenic railway from Curitiba to Morretes, built in the 1880s, runs through the same mountains and is one of the great train rides of Brazil. Antonina and Paranaguá are on the coast beyond.

Campina Grande do Sul, Quatro Barras and Piraquara, on the plateau side, have fuel stations and shops, and there is more in Morretes at the foot. The best months are from April to September, drier and cooler, though mist is always possible.
t.sindhudurg@16.0,73.5:
Shivaji built Sindhudurg on a rock. The fort stands on a small island just off Malvan, on the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, a great enclosure of black stone walls, about three kilometres around, built between 1664 and 1667 to guard against sea raiders and to project the power of the young Maratha state. Its walls rise straight from the surf, with bastions, gateways and hidden entrances, and inside lie temples, wells of fresh water, and the remains of old houses. A short boat ride from Malvan's jetty takes you across, and the view from the ramparts, over the blue Arabian Sea and the coconut-fringed coast, is superb.

The coast road here is a pleasure. The Konkan runs in a long strip between the Western Ghats and the sea, with red laterite soil, cashew and mango orchards, small fishing villages and pale beaches. Roads rise and fall in gentle curves, passing through villages with tiled roofs and temples, and the surface is mostly good, though monsoon rains between June and September can wash out sections and make riding hazardous. The best season is November to February, when the air is dry and the sea breeze cool. March and April are hot, and the Alphonso mangoes that ripen in the orchards, especially around Devgad, are famed across India.

Malvan, under two kilometres away, has nearly nineteen thousand people, so fuel, food and rooms are no problem, and Kudal, about twenty-five kilometres inland, is the larger service town on the main road. Malvan is famous for its cuisine, a spicy, coconut-rich style of cooking centred on fresh fish, prawns and rice, served with a tart red sauce and a flatbread. Eat in a small family restaurant, and you will understand why.

Heading south, the ride continues to Goa, with its Portuguese churches and convents, and north to Vijaydurg, another coastal fort. If you can, stay for sunset and watch the fort turn gold across the water. The walls, the surf and the long, slow light of the evening fill the scene with calm.
t.serras do cordeiro@-25.4,-48.9:
South of Curitiba the Serra do Mar stops being a distant wall and becomes a country of its own, folded into sharp green peaks that rise from the coastal plain of Paraná to well over a thousand metres. The Serras do Cordeiro belong to that mountain tangle, in the zone of protected land and state parks around Pau Oco, near the town of Quatro Barras. Pico Paraná, the highest summit in southern Brazil, and the pyramid of Marumbi are the big names nearby, and the whole range is blanketed by Atlantic forest, a wet, mossy, orchid-hung woodland that catches the clouds coming off the ocean and drips for most of the year.

What strikes a visitor is how abrupt the change is. Within an hour of Curitiba's tidy boulevards you can be in cold fog under tree ferns, with bromeliads on every branch and the sound of water from hidden streams. Howler monkeys, toucans and a great many frogs live here, though the forest is thick enough that you will mostly hear rather than see them. The mountains were also a barrier that made the Paraná coast remote for centuries, and the old roads across them are a story of their own. The Estrada da Graciosa, which links Curitiba with the sea at Antonina, was opened in the nineteenth century, and its cobbled sections and forest hairpins are still among the most beautiful drives in the state.

For a rider this is serious fun. The BR-116 and BR-277 descend from the plateau in long, busy grades with lorries and fog banks, while the Graciosa and the smaller roads wind more gently, with potholes and wet leaves to watch for. Weather is the main variable, because the mountains can swallow the sun in minutes and the temperature falls fast. Winter, from June to August, is cool and sometimes frosty on the plateau, while summer brings warm downpours. Clear days are best in autumn, when the air is crisp.

Quatro Barras, sixteen kilometres away, is a town of about seventeen thousand people and the sensible place for fuel, bread and coffee, and Curitiba has everything else. On the coastal side Morretes serves barreado, a slow-cooked beef stew eaten with manioc flour, which is the classic reward after the descent. Several trails are managed by the state parks authority and require booking or registration, so ask ahead. Carry a rain jacket and a warm layer, and do not leave the marked path, because the forest closes behind you quickly.
t.victorian gothic and art deco ensembles:
Mumbai built itself a seafront in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and the result is one of the most unusual architectural neighbourhoods on earth. The Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles, inscribed by UNESCO in 2018, are two separate groups of buildings, facing each other across the Oval Maidan, a big open cricket ground in the south of the city. On one side are the Gothic Revival buildings of the British Raj: the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, which was Victoria Terminus, the High Court, the University and the Rajabai Clock Tower. On the other are the Art Deco cinemas, hotels and apartment blocks of the 1930s, along Marine Drive.

The station is the star. Its domes, spires, turrets and carved stone details make it look like a cathedral designed by someone who had never been told what a railway was for, and yet it works as a station for millions of commuters every day. The Rajabai Clock Tower, nearby, was modelled on Big Ben, and chimes the hour above the university library. Along Marine Drive, the curve of seafront buildings, in pastel colours and rounded corners, is the evening resort of the whole city, and families come to sit on the sea wall as the sun goes down.

Riding in Mumbai is for the experienced. Traffic is dense, lanes are suggestions and the rain, from June to September, is torrential. Two-wheelers are not permitted on the Bandra-Worli Sea Link, and the rules change, so follow local signs. Mornings and Sundays are the best times for the south of the city, when the streets are quieter and the stone buildings catch the light. Parking is scarce, and it is easier to walk the district.

From the Gateway of India, the Colaba waterfront, ferries cross the harbour to Elephanta Island, whose rock-cut caves, also a World Heritage site, hold a massive carved Shiva. The place shown on the map as Uran lies on the far side of the water, and the road around is long.

Mumbai has fuel and food on every corner. Try a plate of bhel puri on the beach, or a cup of sweet tea at a roadside stall.
t.churches and convents of goa@15.5,73.9:
Goa's early Portuguese rulers built a capital that they hoped would rival Lisbon, and what is left of it, Old Goa, is a group of huge churches rising from tropical green. Albuquerque took the city in 1510, and for the next two centuries it was the centre of Portugal's empire in the East, with a population that may have rivalled London's. Then epidemics and a shifting river drove the people away, the capital moved down the coast, and the great buildings were left standing in a landscape of palms and rice fields. UNESCO listed the Churches and Convents of Goa in 1986.

The Basilica of Bom Jesus is the best known, a plain laterite church with a baroque interior, finished in 1605, that holds the body of Saint Francis Xavier in a silver casket. The Jesuit missionary died in 1552 off the coast of China, and his body was brought here, where it still draws pilgrims, particularly at the saint's feast in early December. Next door, the Sé Cathedral is among the biggest churches in Asia, with a tall tower holding the Golden Bell and an interior of huge white pillars and gilded altars.

The stonework is the thing to notice. The churches are built of laterite, a rusty red stone, and then plastered white, a tropical solution that keeps them cool and gleaming. The carved wooden altarpieces and the painted ceilings are as good as anything in Portugal, and they have the extra interest of Indian craftsmen's hands.

Goa is a place to ride, with palm-lined roads, small villages and a coast of long beaches. Old Goa lies on the Mandovi river, about ten kilometres from Panaji, the state capital, and traffic is moderate, though buses and trucks can be aggressive. Roads are mostly paved but pitted, and from June to September the monsoon turns everything slippery. November to February is dry and pleasant.

Panaji has fuel and food in plenty. The churches are active places of worship, so dress modestly, with covered shoulders and knees, and keep your voice low. A plate of fish curry and rice in a village restaurant is the right way to end the day.
t.shivneri fort@19.2,73.9:
Shivneri is a hill fort above the town of Junnar in the Sahyadri range, and its fame comes from a single event: Shivaji, the founder of the Maratha kingdom, was born here in 1630. The fort stands on a steep, flat-topped hill of black basalt, one of the many Deccan trap formations that give western India its distinctive stepped skyline. Seven gateways, each with strong walls and sharp turns, lead up the slope, and inside the fortifications are cisterns, a small mosque, a temple to the goddess Shivai after whom Shivaji is said to have been named, and a cluster of old buildings, including one said to mark the room of his birth.

The surrounding country is a historian's playground. The Junnar area has more than a hundred rock-cut Buddhist caves, dating from the early centuries of the common era, cut into the basalt hills around the town, including the Lenyadri group, which has a Hindu temple of Ganesha built into one of the caves. The old trade route of the Naneghat pass, one of the earliest Deccan trade routes, leads up from the coastal plain nearby, and the Satavahana dynasty that ruled here left inscriptions that are among the earliest in India.

For the rider, this is a landscape best seen in or just after the monsoon, from July to September, when the hills turn emerald green and waterfalls tumble from every ledge. The roads from Pune, about ninety kilometres to the south, pass through rural Maharashtra with sugarcane fields, grape vineyards and small villages, with a fair amount of truck traffic. The ghat roads climbing toward the Naneghat give some enjoyable curves, though rain can make them slick, and fog may reduce visibility. In the hot season, from March to May, the temperature rises considerably, and the fort climb is better done early in the morning.

Junnar, a town of around twenty-six thousand, has fuel, shops, small restaurants and basic lodging, so you do not need to worry about running out. The climb to the fort involves a long flight of steps, so wear sturdy shoes, bring water and respect the shrine.

The local food is simple and good: misal pav, a spicy sprouted bean curry eaten with bread, and sweet chai from roadside stalls. Dress modestly at the temple and the mosque.
t.gilgit@35.9,74.3:
Gilgit sits in the place where three of the world's greatest mountain systems come together: the Karakoram, the Himalaya and the Hindu Kush. The town lies at roughly fifteen hundred metres in a broad, dry valley at the meeting of the Gilgit and Hunza rivers, with bare brown ridges close on every side, and on a clear day the snow of high peaks hangs over the roofs. Nanga Parbat, the ninth-highest mountain on earth, lies not far south, and from the Hunza side the huge ridge of Rakaposhi appears on the horizon.

This was a key stop on the Silk Road branch that crossed the mountains between China, Kashmir and Central Asia, and the valley has been a Buddhist centre, a Hindu kingdom and a Muslim principality in turn. A Buddha carved into a rock face at Kargah, a few kilometres from town, dates to around the seventh century. In 1931 some of the oldest surviving manuscripts in the world were found near here, Buddhist texts written on birch bark and later known as the Gilgit manuscripts. In more recent times, the town was the capital of a frontier agency of the British Raj, and polo, the local passion, is still played with abandon in the high valleys.

Today Gilgit is the main hub of Gilgit-Baltistan, with a bustling bazaar, a few simple hotels, and the usual loud, cheerful traffic of a Pakistani town. For a rider, it is the main supply base for the Karakoram Highway, which was built by Pakistani and Chinese engineers from the late 1950s to 1978, at the cost of hundreds of workers' lives, and which snakes north along the Hunza valley toward Khunjerab.
