Here you can find fuel, spares, banks, and good food, from fresh apricots in summer to stews of lamb and local bread, with apricot oil and dried fruit sold in the shops.

The road north is paved but battered by rockfall, landslides and the movement of the mountains themselves, and sections can be closed after rain or snow. Expect sharp bends, dust, trucks and cliff edges. The best months are May to October, when the passes are open and the days warm, but nights can be cold. Security and road conditions can change, so check locally and ask about permits and any restrictions before setting out. Fill up and stock water here, because the next big town lies a good distance away.
t.ak baital pass@38.6,73.6:
The Ak-Baital Pass, at 4,655 metres, is the highest point on the Pamir Highway, and it looks the part: a bare, windswept saddle of grey and tan rock, with no trees, no plants and scarcely any life except the odd marmot, on a high plateau where the sky seems dark blue even at noon. The name means White Horse, and the story is that a white horse once crossed here and left no tracks, though no one can say when. The road climbs from the east across a long, rough plateau and drops to the west toward Karakul, with the borders of China and Kyrgyzstan not far away.

The highway itself is a piece of history. The Pamir road, or M41, was built by the Soviets in the 1930s on the line of an ancient caravan track, a branch of the Silk Road, linking Osh in Kyrgyzstan with Khorog in Tajikistan across the roof of the world. In the nineteenth century, the Pamirs were the scene of the Great Game, the rivalry between Britain and Russia for control of Central Asia, and explorers crossed these plateaus with caravans of yaks and horses. Lake Karakul, a little beyond the pass, lies in a basin formed by a meteorite that struck about five million years ago, and its water is a deep blue-black, rimmed by white peaks.

The riding is tough and remote. The surface is a mix of broken asphalt, gravel and sandy stretches, with potholes, washouts and sections of corrugation, and the altitude affects both rider and machine. A carburetted engine will run rich and weak, and fuel injection helps a little, but expect a loss of power. Altitude sickness is a serious risk, so acclimatise first, ascend slowly and descend if symptoms worsen. Weather can change in minutes, and snow can fall in any month. The road is passable mostly from May to October.

The nearest services are at Murghab, the highest town in Tajikistan, at about 3,650 metres, and at Karakul, where fuel can be uncertain, so carry spare fuel and extra supplies. A permit for the Gorno-Badakhshan region is required and should be arranged before travelling.

Stop for a moment at the cairn and prayer flags, take a photograph and a few deep breaths, and remember to be patient with yourself. The silence is enormous, and the horizon is a ring of ice.
t.yamchun@37.0,72.2:
The Panj river is the border here, and across the water the land is Afghanistan. At Yamchun, in the Wakhan valley of Tajikistan, the road runs high above the river on the Tajik side, and the other bank is a narrow ribbon of farms and mud-brick houses under the great wall of the Hindu Kush. The valley is one of the most remote inhabited places in Asia, and its people, the Wakhi and Pamiri, are largely Ismaili Muslims who have lived here for many centuries, farming barley and apricots in small terraced fields.

Yamchun Fort is the great monument. A ruined fortress of stone and mud-brick on a rocky spur above the river, it dates from the third century BC and was part of a chain of strongholds that guarded the old caravan route between China, India and Central Asia, and the view from its ramparts across the valley is long and dramatic. Close by, the hot springs of Bibi Fatima, said to be good for women's ailments, bubble up in a small stone bath, and local people use them regularly. The fortress and the springs are about a hundred metres apart in height and a short walk, and both are worth the trouble.

The riding on the Wakhan road is rough, slow and tremendous. The route follows the Panj, with a mix of dirt, gravel and broken asphalt, with washouts, rockfalls and sudden stream crossings, and the surface changes every few kilometres. Dust, heat in summer and cold at night are normal, and the altitude is moderate, around three thousand metres, but enough to tire you. A permit for the Gorno-Badakhshan region is needed, and is best arranged in advance, and the border zone requires care and respect.

Fuel is a serious issue, since stations are few and supplies uncertain, so fill the tank in Khorog, carry extra if possible and ask at each village. Food is available at homestays, where families serve bread, tea, soup and yoghurt, and the hospitality is generous. Accommodation is in Pamiri houses with their distinctive roof structures and a warm central room.

Take time at the fort. In the early morning, the light turns the valley gold, the river is quiet and the air smells of dust and apricots. The mountains on the Afghan side look near enough to touch, and the peace of the place is hard to forget.
t.langar@37.1,72.7:
Langar is the last real village of the Tajik Wakhan, a cluster of stone and mud-brick houses at about 2,800 metres, hemmed in by the Panj river on one side and the high, bare mountains on the other, and beyond it the valley narrows toward the Wakhjir pass and China. It is a village of orchards and walled fields, irrigated by channels from the mountains, and in the evening smoke rises from every roof and children play on the dirt lanes. Across the river, in Afghanistan, a faint track runs along the foot of the Hindu Kush, and one sometimes sees a donkey or a man on a motorbike on the other bank.

The people here are Pamiri Ismailis, and their houses are built to a traditional plan, with a single main room under a roof of five carved wooden pillars, each said to represent a person of the faith. The village is also known for its petroglyphs. On a hillside above, thousands of carvings of ibex, hunters and symbols have been scratched into the dark rock over many centuries, and a short walk up the slope leads to the best of them. The animal figures, with their curved horns, look surprisingly lively. Marco Polo is believed to have passed through the Wakhan in the thirteenth century on his way to China, and the route was an important one for travellers and traders.

The road from Khorog to Langar is long, rough and slow, and the surface alternates between broken tarmac and gravel, with plenty of dust. It follows the Panj for most of the way, through a series of villages and fortresses, with views over the border. Sections can be washed out by floods or buried by rockfalls, and bridges are sometimes basic. A permit for the Gorno-Badakhshan region is required, and the weather can be hot in the day and freezing at night, so pack accordingly. The best time is from June to September.

Fuel is a concern, as there are very few stations along the valley, so carry extra, ask locally and fill up when you can. Food and shelter are available in homestays, which serve fresh bread, soup, apricots and tea, and a bed and a meal are modestly priced. Do not expect a shop with much choice.

If you have a day to spare, walk to the petroglyphs in the evening, when the light is low and the valley is quiet. It is a small place at the end of a long road, and it feels like the edge of the world.
t.karakul@39.0,73.5:
At about 3,900 metres, Karakul is high enough that you will notice every step. The lake lies in a bleak, enormous basin in the eastern Pamirs of Tajikistan, a sheet of cold, salty, turquoise water ringed by bare brown mountains and white peaks, with the Chinese border not far off. It filled the crater left by a meteorite that struck the Earth some five million years ago, according to the geologists, which explains its odd, nearly round shape and its lack of any outlet. No fish live here, the water being too salty, and in the early morning the surface can be glassy and still.

The village on the shore is a scatter of low mud-brick houses, a few shops and the homestays that serve travellers on the Pamir Highway. Life is hard here. Winter temperatures drop to forty below, the wind is constant, and the people, mostly Kyrgyz herders, survive on yaks, sheep and trade with passing trucks. Even in summer the nights are bitterly cold, and a homestay with a coal stove and a pile of blankets is a blessing. Meals are simple: bread, tea, soup, perhaps some fried potatoes.

The road is the legendary M41, the Pamir Highway, running from Osh to Khorog and crossing some of the highest passes in the world. To the north it climbs over the Kyzyl-Art Pass, at about 4,280 metres, which marks the border with Kyrgyzstan, and to the south the Ak-Baital Pass, at 4,655 metres, is the highest on the route. Surfaces are variable, from decent asphalt to broken, rutted patches and corrugated gravel, and the thin air robs engines of power and riders of patience. Altitude sickness is a real risk, so ascend slowly, drink plenty of water and be ready to descend if you feel unwell.

Fuel is the serious question. Karakul has little, and supplies are patchy and often of poor quality, so carry extra in jerry cans and plan carefully. The larger town of Murghab, to the south, is the main supply point. Border permits and the special GBAO permit are required, so check the rules in advance.

Dawn here is the best moment. The light spreads over the lake, the peaks turn pink and gold, and the silence is so complete that the click of a cooling engine seems loud.
t.ishkashim@36.7,71.6:
A river a few hundred metres wide is all that separates Tajikistan from Afghanistan at Ishkashim, and you can watch farmers on the other bank working their fields as you drink your tea. The Panj, the upper Amu Darya, runs through a broad green valley here, hemmed in by the great ranges of the Pamir to the north and the Hindu Kush to the south. Snow peaks stand across the water, close enough to count the ridges, and the sight is among the most dramatic on the whole Pamir route. The town is small, around a few thousand people, with a bazaar, a handful of guesthouses and a border crossing that opens for traders and aid vehicles.

This is the entrance to the Wakhan Corridor, the narrow strip of land that stretches east toward China, created as a buffer between the British and Russian empires in the nineteenth century. Marco Polo is believed to have passed this way on his journey east, and the Silk Road caravans did for centuries. The people are Pamiri, mostly Ismaili Muslims who follow the Aga Khan, and they speak languages unrelated to Tajik. Hospitality is a point of pride, and a rider who stops will be offered tea and bread before long.

Heading east from town, the road along the Panj is spectacular and demanding. It is a mix of rough asphalt, gravel and stretches of track, running at the foot of cliffs and between fields of barley, apricot and poplar. The Wakhan road to Langar passes ruined fortresses, such as the one at Yamchun, with views across to Afghan villages. Rivers cross the road, and some bridges are narrow. Hot springs at Garm Chashma, a short side trip, are a welcome treat after a long day. Rain is rare, but the sun is intense, the wind can be brutal and the dust gets everywhere.

Fuel needs planning. Ishkashim has little, and its supply is variable, while Khorog, to the north-west, is the larger regional centre with proper stations, banks and shops. Carry extra fuel in the Wakhan, as distances between supply points are long. A GBAO permit is required, and you should check the current conditions on the Afghan border, which can change.

A Saturday market was once held on the border itself, where Afghans and Tajiks traded goods from a tent. The market's status has varied, but the thought of two countries meeting over a river is a fine memory to take away.
t.malvan@16.1,73.5:
Malvan is a fishing town on the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, where the Western Ghats come down close to the Arabian Sea and the land is a strip of red earth, coconut palms and rocky coves. The town is crowded and noisy, with a busy fish market, narrow streets and a harbour full of painted wooden boats, but it is the gateway to some of the best coastline in western India. It has a character all its own, and the local people are proud of their food and their language.

The big attraction is the sea fort of Sindhudurg, which stands on a rocky island just off the shore, reached by a short boat ride from the harbour. Built in the 1660s under the Maratha leader Shivaji, it has thick walls of black stone, bastions, and a long, curved sea wall, and it was designed to guard the coast against the Portuguese, the British and pirates. Inside are temples, wells and a small shrine said to hold a footprint of Shivaji. A little way south is Tarkarli, with a long white beach and clear water, popular for snorkelling and diving.

Malvani cooking is worth a stop in itself. It is a spicy, coconut-based cuisine with plenty of fresh fish, prawns and crab, and the classic meal is a fish thali with rice, curry and fried fish, served with sol kadhi, a pink drink of kokum and coconut milk. Many small restaurants near the harbour serve it, and the prices are modest. Nearby Devgad is famous for its Alphonso mangoes, which ripen in April and May and are widely regarded as among the best in India.

The ride along the coast is a joy, with winding roads through villages, palm groves and paddy fields, over rivers on small bridges, and past hills with views down to the sea. The surface can be uneven, with potholes after the monsoon, and local traffic includes buses, autorickshaws and cattle, so keep your speed down. The monsoon, from June to September, brings heavy rain and many closures, and the best season is between October and March. Malvan has fuel stations on the main road, and it is wise to fill up here, since services are sparser on the lanes to the south.
t.alibag@18.6,72.9:
Alibag is the unofficial seaside of Mumbai, a small town on the Konkan coast, a short ferry ride and a longer road trip from the city, where the Mumbaikars go to escape on weekends. The town is low-key, with a long, dark-sand beach, coconut groves and a few old colonial-era buildings, and the pace is slower than you would expect given the size of the city across the water. It feels more like a village that has been dressed up for visitors, and it keeps a few of its old habits.

The main sight is Kolaba Fort, which stands on a rock in the sea, a short way off the beach. At low tide, you can walk to it across the wet sand, through shallow water, and at high tide the fort is cut off. The fort was built in the seventeenth century, under the Maratha leader Shivaji, and later became the base of the admiral Kanhoji Angre, who commanded a powerful fleet and controlled the coast for decades. Inside the walls are a few temples, wells and a freshwater pond, and the view back toward the town is worth the walk.

The ride along the coast is easy, with flat roads, palm groves and small fishing villages, and a few interesting stops, including the old Portuguese fort at Revdanda and the beaches at Nagaon and Kihim. The roads are usually good, though traffic on weekends can be heavy, with cars, buses and motorbikes from Mumbai all heading in the same direction. The surface can be broken after the monsoon, and the heat in April and May is intense. The best months are from October to February, when the weather is dry and cool.

Alibag has about twenty thousand people, and fuel, food and supplies are plentiful. There are many seafood restaurants near the beach and in the town, serving fresh fish, prawns and crab, with rice and coconut curry, and a good many places to buy cold drinks and coconut water. If you arrive by ferry from Mumbai, the road to the town is short, and a ride south along the coast is the natural next step.
t.serra do corvo branco@-28.0,-49.4:
The Serra do Corvo Branco is a road cut through solid rock, and the walls on either side are so high that the sky narrows to a strip. The route was cut through the escarpment in recent decades, leaving sheer cliffs of sandstone and basalt towering above the track, in places tens of metres tall. It lies in the highlands of Santa Catarina, near the town of Urubici, an area that has the coldest winters in Brazil and where frost and occasional snow are normal between June and August.

The surrounding country is the planalto serrano, an upland of rolling grassland, araucaria pine and deep canyons, cut by sudden escarpments that fall toward the coast. The araucaria, with its candelabra branches, is a survivor from the age of the dinosaurs, and its seeds, the pinhão, are a favourite winter snack, roasted or boiled. Lookouts along the rim give views over canyons, waterfalls and layers of mist, and the sea of cloud that fills the valleys on cold mornings is one of the most famous sights of the region. At around 1,470 metres, the air is cool and clear.

The road is a gravel and dirt track, narrow and steep in places, with a loose surface, sharp bends and wet patches. Rain can turn the surface to slippery clay quickly, and fog can come down within minutes, hiding the edge. It is a route for an experienced rider on a dual-sport or adventure bike, preferably with a companion, and anyone in doubt should ask locals about conditions. The nearby Serra do Rio do Rastro, a famous tarmac road of countless hairpins down to the coast, provides a smoother and busier alternative.

Services are in Urubici, which has fuel, hotels, and plenty of restaurants serving grilled meat and local cheese, and in Lauro Müller and Grão-Pará. There is nothing on the pass itself, so fill up, carry water and tell someone your plan. Early morning, with frost on the grass and the sun lighting the cliffs, is the best time.
t.lulusar lake@35.1,73.9:
Lulusar sits in a cup of high mountains at the head of the Kaghan Valley, at somewhere around 3,400 metres, and when you first see it the colour looks wrong: a deep, cold blue lying against grey scree and snowfields as if someone had spilled ink between the peaks. The lake is the source of the Kunhar River, which runs down through Naran and eventually joins the Jhelum, and the road to Babusar Pass runs right along its shore. It is one of those places where you are glad to have a stop planned, because the surface is usually mirror-calm in the early morning and full of reflected mountains.

Riding this far up the valley is an adventure in itself. From Naran the road climbs past Besal through wide meadows, then up into a barren high country where trees disappear and the wind tastes of snow. The tarmac is patchy, mostly paved but with sections broken by meltwater and landslides, and the way is shared with jeeps, buses and herders moving flocks. Oxygen is thinner than you expect, so go slowly, drink water, and do not rush: a rider who feels dizzy at this height should stop and rest rather than push on.

Lulusar belongs to the season. The road and the pass beyond are generally open only in summer, roughly from June into the autumn, and snow can close it early or late. In July and August the grass is green and the shepherds' huts are occupied, and in September the light turns clear and sharp. Weather changes fast; a morning of blue sky can turn to sleet by afternoon, so carry warm layers and waterproofs even in high summer. Local people are generally welcoming, and tea at a roadside shack is a better idea than it sounds when your fingers are cold.

Naran, behind you, is the place to fill the tank and buy supplies, and you should carry spare fuel if you plan to cross over toward Chilas on the other side. Simple food and hot tea are available at small stalls in the warmer months, but do not rely on them. The silence at the water, broken only by wind and the occasional bell on a goat, is the real attraction, and it is worth ten minutes of just standing still.
t.babusar pass@35.1,74.1:
At around 4,173 metres, Babusar is one of the great high crossings of the Pakistani north, and the satisfaction of reaching it is slightly out of proportion to the hardware you find at the top: a gate, a few tea stalls, some prayer flags and rocks, and a wind that could take your hat to the next valley. The pass links the Kaghan Valley with the Indus gorge at Chilas, on the Karakoram Highway, and it has served as a shortcut between the two for centuries. Traders, herders and later military patrols all used the crossing, and its name is tied to that older traffic.

The road up from the Kaghan side comes through the bleak, open uplands past Lulusar Lake, a gradual climb with the occasional steep section, and you feel the air thin as you go. The other side is the dramatic one. The descent toward Chilas drops in a long series of hairpins down a bare, brown mountainside, with huge views over the valley and, when the haze permits, Nanga Parbat, the ninth highest mountain in the world, standing far off to the north. The surface is paved but battered by snow and rockfall, so keep your speed down, stay wide of the drops, and expect to meet buses, jeeps and trucks coming around the bends.

The pass is a summer road, usually open from about June to October, and it can close suddenly after snow. Always check locally before committing to it, since conditions vary from season to season and from one week to the next. Late summer mornings tend to be clearest. Weather at 4,000 metres is not forgiving: a sunny start can end in cold rain, and headaches and breathlessness are real, so take your time and spend a few minutes at the top acclimatising before pushing on.

Fill at Naran before you climb, or at Chilas if you are coming from the other side, and carry a spare can because the distance between pumps is long on rough roads. Tea, noodles and biscuits can be had from stalls at the summit when the season is on. It is a basic stop, but the combination of altitude and open mountains makes it a place riders remember long after the details of the road have faded.
t.serra do rio do rastro@-28.4,-49.5:
The Serra do Rio do Rastro is a wall of rock between the coast and the highlands of Santa Catarina, and the road that climbs it is one of the great sights of southern Brazil. The escarpment is part of the Serra Geral, a long edge where the Atlantic plateau drops to the lowlands, and the road scales it in a tangle of hairpins. From the top, at about 1,400 metres, the view drops to a coastal plain and, on a clear day, to the sea. Cloud often drifts through the bends, and the road appears and disappears like a ribbon in the mist.

The road was built in the 1930s to link the coal-mining area around Lauro Müller with the plateau, and it has been rebuilt and improved since. The coal towns below, such as Lauro Müller, Orleans and Siderópolis, grew from mining and from the settlement of European immigrants, mostly Germans and Italians, whose descendants still shape the food and architecture of the region. On the plateau above, the air is cooler and the landscape turns to araucaria forest and open grassland, with pines standing like umbrellas.

For riders, the climb is the main attraction. The bends are tight and frequent, with the road switching back on itself again and again, and the surface is generally paved but can be damp and slippery. Mist and fog are common and can reduce visibility to a few metres, so it is better to go in clear weather and ride with care. Trucks use the road, so overtaking requires judgment, and viewpoints along the way are good places to stop and check the view. In winter, frost and even snow can appear on the plateau, and the temperature difference between the coast and the top can be large.

Fuel is available in Lauro Müller, about fifteen kilometres from the climb, and in other towns along the way, but services are limited on the plateau, so fill up before you go. Small restaurants and stalls near the viewpoints sell snacks and coffee, and the regional cuisine includes pinhão, the seed of the araucaria, boiled in winter, and hearty meat dishes.

Brazil drives on the right, and local drivers can be fast, so keep to your line and stay alert on blind bends. The nearby Serra do Corvo Branco, a road cut through rock walls near Urubici, makes a dramatic companion loop.
t.kas plateau@17.2,73.7:
For most of the year, Kas is a bare, rocky plateau of black basalt, and then the monsoon arrives. Within weeks, from late August into September, the laterite surface is covered in a carpet of tiny wildflowers, in pink, yellow, purple and white, with balsams, orchids, sundews and species found nowhere else on earth. The plateau lies in the Western Ghats, a range with so many endemic plants and animals that it is one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, and it was included in the UNESCO listing in 2012. Locals call it the Valley of Flowers of Maharashtra.

The blooms are delicate. Each flower grows in a thin layer of soil on the rock, and the whole system depends on the rains. To protect it, visitors are limited each day, a ticket is required, and walkers must stay on the paths, because stepping on the flowers can destroy the crop for the season. The best times are early morning and late afternoon, when the light is soft and the crowds are fewer. Fog is common, and the lake of Kas, a small reservoir nearby, often lies hidden in mist.

The road up from Satara, about twenty-five kilometres to the east, is a steady climb through forest, with hairpins and views over the Koyna valley and the Sahyadri hills. The surface is usually good, though heavy rain can cause potholes and landslides, and the road is slippery with mud and leaves in the monsoon. Weekend traffic in flower season can be heavy, so a weekday visit is a better idea. Waterfalls appear everywhere during the rains, and the nearby Thoseghar falls are among the best.

Fuel is available in Satara, so fill the tank there, as villages near the plateau are small. Simple meals are sold by local families at stalls along the road, with hot tea, corn and fried snacks. Carry a rain jacket and non-slip boots. The ride that begins here links the hill fort of Panhala with the sea fort of Vijaydurg, taking you from the mountains to the Konkan coast, and the mood changes with every few hundred metres of altitude.
t.sary tash@39.7,73.3:
Sary-Tash is a handful of low houses and a few guesthouses at a crossroads in southern Kyrgyzstan, at about 3,100 metres, and it has a lot of importance for a place so small. Here the road from Osh, coming south over the passes, meets the route that turns east to China at Irkeshtam and the one that turns south to the Pamir Highway and Tajikistan. In the old days, caravans on the Silk Road passed through, and the Soviet Union later built the road that is still the main artery of the region.

The setting is magnificent. To the south, the Alay valley opens out into a broad, high plain of pale grass, with the snowy wall of the Trans-Alay range beyond, the northern edge of the Pamirs. On clear days, Peak Lenin, at more than seven thousand metres, shows above the ridge, and the view is among the great mountain panoramas of Central Asia. The air is thin, dry and cold, with a clean, grassy smell, and the wind can be fierce.

Riding in this region is a serious proposition. The road from Osh climbs over the Taldyk pass to get here, and the Kyzyl-Art pass lies farther south on the way toward Tajikistan; the surface is partly paved, partly rough, with potholes, landslides and sections of gravel. Weather changes fast, with snow possible in any month, and the high passes are closed or dangerous in winter. Cars and trucks are few, and livestock and shepherds on the road are common. Nights are cold, and even in summer the temperature can drop below freezing. The best time to come is roughly June to September, and altitude can bring headaches and fatigue.

There are limited services. Sary-Tash has a few guesthouses and homestays that offer tea, bread, soup and a bed, and a couple of simple shops, and fuel is available in small quantities from roadside sellers and a basic station, though quality and supply can be uncertain. It is wise to carry extra fuel, water and food, and to fill whenever you can. Mobile signal comes and goes, and border permits may be needed for the routes toward Tajikistan and China, so check requirements in advance.

Warm tea with bread and honey in a guesthouse is the right welcome after the cold ride, and the generosity of the Kyrgyz herders and hosts is one of the best things about the region.
t.lauro muller@-28.4,-49.4:
Lauro Müller is a coal-mining town at the foot of the Serra do Rio do Rastro, one of the most famous roads in Brazil, and it sits in a quiet, green valley under a wall of cliffs. The town of ten thousand has a modest, working look, with a railway that once carried coal to the coast and the faded colour of an industry that has declined. The name honours Lauro Müller, a Brazilian engineer and politician born in this region in the nineteenth century, who served as governor of the state and later as a government minister.

The mountain behind the town is the attraction. The Serra do Rio do Rastro is an escarpment where the high plateau of southern Brazil drops sharply toward the coast, and the road climbs it in a spectacular series of switchbacks, with about two hundred and eighty-four bends cut into the slope. The road rises roughly a thousand metres in a short distance, and from the viewpoint near the top you can see the whole serpentine ribbon below, with the coastal plain stretching to the sea in the distance. On clear days, the panorama takes your words away.

The bends are tight, and the surface is generally good, but traffic can be heavy with trucks that crawl up the slope, and tourists who stop for photographs. In the early morning, fog often fills the valley, and when the sun breaks through, the cloud sinks below the road like a white sea. Rain makes the surface slick, and in winter, temperatures at the top can fall close to freezing, with the occasional dusting of snow. Ride up in the morning for the best light and the least traffic.

Another remarkable road in the region is Corvo Branco, a road cut through the rock of the escarpment between walls that tower high above the vehicles, with a dramatic view out over the canyon. It is reached from the plateau side and is a popular excursion.

Lauro Müller has fuel stations, small shops, bakeries and simple restaurants, and nearby Orleans and Urussanga offer more choice. The local food includes sausage, polenta and wine, a legacy of Italian settlers who came to this part of Santa Catarina. The best time to ride is autumn and spring, with clear air and moderate temperatures.
t.goa panaji@15.5,73.8:
Panaji is Goa's compact capital, on the south bank of the Mandovi river where it meets the Arabian Sea, and it is a quieter, tidier place than most Indian state capitals. Portugal ruled Goa for more than four hundred years until India took it in December 1961, and the old colonial feel survives in the red-roofed houses, the balconies with carved wood and the Latin names on shop signs. The best-known district is Fontainhas, a small quarter of narrow lanes and painted villas in yellow, blue and green, where Portuguese-style bakeries sell sweet bebinca and the church of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception looks down on a zigzag white staircase.

A short way east, at Old Goa, the former capital was abandoned after epidemics and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with huge churches and convents. The Basilica of Bom Jesus holds the body of Saint Francis Xavier, which is brought out for viewing every decade or so. Goan food is a mix of Portuguese and Konkan flavours, with fish curry and rice, spicy xacuti, pork vindaloo, which came from the Portuguese dish vinha d'alhos, and fresh seafood grilled with chilli. Feni, a spirit distilled from cashew fruit or coconut sap, is the local drink.

Panaji is the finish of the Konkan coast road, which follows the Arabian Sea down from Maharashtra, with a succession of ferries, bridges, headlands and beaches under coconut palms. The riding is rewarding but unpredictable, with a good surface on the main highway, patches of potholes and sudden speed breakers on others, and lots of cows, dogs, scooters and buses. Keep to the left, ride in daylight if possible, and expect the unexpected. The monsoon from June to September brings heavy rain and landslides on the hill sections, and the best season is November to February.

Fuel is easy in a city of sixty-five thousand, with stations on all the main roads and across the bridges to Porvorim. Cafés serve strong coffee and fresh bread, and the riverside promenade is a pleasant place to stop in the evening, with a breeze off the water and the casino boats lit up. Look for a hotel with a safe place for the bike, and be careful with scooters, which are easy to rent but need a valid licence.
t.koyna wildlife sanctuary@17.2,73.7:
Koyna Wildlife Sanctuary covers a long, rugged stretch of the Western Ghats in the Satara district of Maharashtra, around the Koyna reservoir, which the locals call Shivsagar. The dam across the Koyna river was built in the 1950s and 60s to produce hydroelectric power, and the lake behind it now stretches for more than sixty kilometres through the hills, one of the largest in the state. In December 1967 an earthquake of magnitude 6.3 struck near the dam, killing nearly two hundred people, and it is one of the best-known examples of earthquakes thought to be triggered by a reservoir.

The land around is a green wall, part of the Sahyadri range that UNESCO listed as a World Heritage Site in 2012 for its biodiversity. The slopes are covered in semi-evergreen forest, with teak, ironwood and giant bamboo, and in the monsoon waterfalls pour down every rock face. The sanctuary and the neighbouring Chandoli National Park form the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve, home to leopards, Indian gaur, sambar, giant squirrels and a small number of tigers. The birds are rich too, with hornbills and the Malabar whistling thrush, whose song is a gentle, human-like whistle at dawn.

The riding is in the Ghats themselves, on narrow mountain roads that climb in hairpins and drop to the Konkan coast. A road through the Koyna valley connects Satara with Chiplun on the coast, with long rainforest stretches, tight bends and little traffic, though in the monsoon landslides, fallen branches and fog can be a serious problem. The best time is October to February, when the air is clear and the grass is green, and the hot season from March to May is dusty. Be careful at dusk, when animals cross the road and the light fades quickly.

This is remote country, so plan fuel carefully. The nearest town is Koynanagar, about twenty-six kilometres away, which has some services, but the larger towns of Satara and Karad are safer bets for a full tank. There are a few small hotels and forest rest houses near the dam, and food is simple, mostly rice, lentils and fresh vegetables. Carry water and a rain jacket, and check with the forest department about access, as parts of the sanctuary are restricted for conservation.
t.radhanagari wildlife sanctuary@17.2,73.7:
So the landscape here is the same crumpled green wall of the Western Ghats, only a little to the north of the place itself. The country is high plateau cut by steep ravines, with laterite caps, forests of ironwood and jamun, and grass that turns gold by January.

Radhanagari is best known as a home of the Indian gaur, the huge dark bison that stands almost two metres at the shoulder, and in the sanctuary you can sometimes see herds moving through the clearings at dusk. The dam at the edge of the reserve was built early in the twentieth century on the orders of Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur, a ruler remembered for schools, hostels and reforms. It was an advanced work for its time and still supplies water to the region. Dajipur, inside the sanctuary, has forest rest houses and watchtowers, and in the rains the whole area is wrapped in mist and waterfalls.

The ride runs down off the Ghats toward the coast at Vijaydurg, a sea fort on the Sindhudurg coast whose walls were extended by Shivaji and which was one of the great naval bases of the Maratha fleet. The road crosses the range by one of the ghat passes, the Phonda Ghat among them, dropping several hundred metres in a series of tight hairpins through dense forest and then into a coastal landscape of cashew and mango groves, red laterite soil and white-sand beaches. The surface is mostly good, but the hairpins are steep, trucks come down slowly, and fog or rain can reduce visibility to a few metres.

Out here, services are limited. Fill before the climb. A small stall by the road will give you hot tea and fried bhaji, a welcome thing in cold wet weather, and in March the mango blossom perfumes the whole coast. Avoid the heavy monsoon, and travel in the cool dry months.
t.chandoli national park@17.2,73.7:
Chandoli became a national park in 2004, which makes it young by Indian standards, but the forest it protects has been growing in the Sahyadri hills since long before the idea of parks existed. It lies in Sangli and Kolhapur districts of Maharashtra, around the reservoir of the Warna river, and it links with Koyna to the south to form the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve, one of the main wild corridors of the northern Western Ghats.

What you see is the scarp of the Ghats in all its drama, with sheer basalt cliffs, laterite plateaus that blaze with wildflowers after the monsoon, and thick forests of ain, jamun and wild mango in the valleys. Tigers have been moving back into the park in recent years, though you are far likelier to see Indian gaur, sambar, barking deer and giant squirrels, and in the evenings the calls of Malabar whistling thrushes and hornbills fill the trees. On the ridges, the old hill fort of Prachitgad stands within the area, a ruined Maratha stronghold reached by a rough track.

The roads that cross the range are what a rider comes for. They drop from the plateau to the Konkan coast in a series of tight bends and sudden views, with waterfalls pouring off the cliff in the rains and mist covering the road at dawn. The surface is a mixture of tarmac and patched concrete, and bridges can be narrow and slippery. After heavy monsoon rain, landslides and fallen trees are common, and local people will happily tell you which stretches are blocked. Dusk brings animals to the roadside, so avoid riding after dark.

Plan your fuel in Karad, Satara or Kolhapur, the larger towns on the plateau, and carry water. Small stalls serve tea and vada pav, the Maharashtrian answer to a burger, and homestays near the park offer rice, lentils and a very hot red chutney. Entry to the park is controlled by the Forest Department, so check what is open, and go between November and February for clear skies and cool days.
t.bom jardim da serra@-28.3,-49.6:
Bom Jardim da Serra sits on the high plateau of Santa Catarina, a cold, windswept, rolling grassland dotted with araucaria pines and apple orchards, at the very top of the Serra Geral escarpment. It is a small place, and the larger towns are close: Lauro Muller, about ten thousand people, lies at the foot of the escarpment, and Sao Joaquim, sixteen thousand, is up the plateau and known as one of the coldest towns in Brazil, where snow falls in some winters. Fuel and services are in those towns, so plan accordingly.

The ride is the reason to come. The road up the Serra do Rio do Rastro is one of the great motorcycle roads of Brazil, a ribbon of tarmac that climbs the face of a huge sandstone and basalt escarpment in dozens of hairpin bends, with sheer drops, long views over the lowlands and the sea in the distance. At the top, the plateau opens into broad, flowing roads through grassland and forest, ideal for relaxed riding. Fog and cloud often fill the lowlands below, producing a sea of clouds, a sight that makes riders stop and stare. The Serra do Corvo Branco, a nearby gravel road cut through rock walls in a deep canyon, is a more adventurous option, with tall cliffs on both sides, and care is needed in wet weather.

The plateau has a history of cattle drovers. For centuries, muleteers moved herds across the highlands to markets in the south, and the old tropeiro routes shaped the towns, with their wooden churches and slow rhythm. Italian and German settlers farmed the lower valleys, and the apple industry came later, with the cool climate suiting orchards. The local cuisine includes pinhao, the nut of the araucaria pine, boiled or roasted in winter, and hearty barbecued meat, with chimarrao, the bitter herbal tea, passed around in a gourd.

Nature is dramatic. The araucaria, or Paraná pine, is an ancient tree with an umbrella-shaped crown, and its forests are home to rare birds. Frost is common in winter, and the grassland turns pale gold. The air is cold and clean, and the evenings are chilly even in summer.

Bring a warm jacket, gloves and a waterproof layer, since fog and rain are common and the temperature can drop sharply. Ride carefully on the descent, where the road is steep, narrow and often wet.
t.sary tash@39.7,73.2:
Sary-Tash is a crossroads at the top of the world, a straggle of low houses, yurt camps and cargo trucks at a little over three thousand metres in the southern Alay valley of Kyrgyzstan. Three roads meet here: the one north to Osh, a long day away, the Pamir Highway climbing southwest toward Tajikistan, and the track east to the Chinese border at Irkeshtam. The name means yellow stone, and the colour comes from the dry grass and the dusty hills. Nothing else for a long way is bigger, which is why every overland traveller seems to stop.

The riding is a mix of epic and exhausting. From Osh, the highway climbs through green foothills and over the Taldyk Pass before dropping into the Alay valley, a wide, high, windswept trough of grassland, with the wall of the Pamir-Alay range along the southern side. The road is mostly tarmac, with sections of rough surface, potholes and washouts after rain or snow. Altitude affects riders and engines alike, so take time to acclimatise and carry warm gear, since temperatures can plunge even in summer. Fuel is sold in the village, though quality varies and supplies can run short, so top up in Osh and carry spare if you can. The best season is June to September, but snow and hail can arrive in any month.

The real show is on the skyline. On a clear morning, the long white wall of the Trans-Alay range, topped by Lenin Peak at more than seven thousand metres, rises above the valley to the south, so close that it looks like a painted backdrop. The air is thin, dry and extremely clear, and the light is fierce. Herders drive yaks, horses and sheep across the valley, and in summer, nomad families set up yurts on the pasture, offering tea, bread and fermented mare's milk to passers-by.

Sary-Tash is a place with a long memory of travel. The old Silk Road passed through here, with caravans carrying silk, spices and other goods between China and Central Asia, and the Pamir Highway was upgraded by Soviet engineers in the 1930s as a military and trade road. Today the village is a stop for overlanders, truckers on the China route and climbers heading for base camp.

Accommodation is basic: homestays with a warm stove and a plate of plov, or a yurt with felt blankets. Bring a sleeping bag, cash in Kyrgyz som, snacks and plenty of water, and be prepared for cold nights and a long ride.
t.florianopolis@-27.6,-48.5:
Florianópolis is mostly an island, and the island has more beaches than anybody can reasonably visit. The city sits on and around Santa Catarina Island, joined to the mainland by bridges, among them the Hercílio Luz, a steel suspension bridge opened in 1926 that is the city's symbol and now closed to vehicles. About four hundred thousand people live here, in a mix of high-rise centre, lagoon-side suburbs and old fishing villages, and the local nickname, Magic Island, comes from its mix of surf, forest and the folklore of the early Azorean settlers.

Those Portuguese settlers from the Azores arrived in the eighteenth century, and their influence remains in the architecture of villages like Ribeirão da Ilha and Santo Antônio de Lisboa, with their low colonial houses, whitewashed churches and waterside restaurants. Oysters and shrimp are the local specialty, and the island is the centre of Brazilian oyster farming, which means seafood is fresh and affordable. The Lagoa da Conceição, a big lagoon framed by dunes and hills, is the hub of nightlife and sports.

Riding here is easier than you might expect. Roads follow the coast around the island, with views of sea, dunes and forested hills, and heading south on the BR-101 on the mainland, the highway runs through coastal plain, with eucalyptus, rice paddies and small towns, toward Praia do Rosa. Traffic, though, can be heavy in the high season from December to February, when the city fills with visitors from Argentina and the rest of Brazil, so early starts are wise. Wet roads and sand on the tarmac are hazards near the beaches.

As a city of this size, Florianópolis has all the fuel, workshops and food a rider needs, and Morro da Cruz and Saco dos Limões are among the neighbourhoods close to the centre. Try a plate of fresh oysters or a seafood stew called a moqueca, and take a walk on one of the quieter beaches before you head on. Weather is warm and humid in summer, mild in winter, with the odd cold wind from the south.
t.praia do rosa@-28.1,-48.6:
Praia do Rosa is a curve of sand backed by green hills, a lagoon and a handful of wooden houses, and it has attracted surfers, artists and travellers for decades. It lies in the municipality of Imbituba on the southern coast of Santa Catarina, about thirteen kilometres from the town, and it has resisted the high-rise development you see farther north. The beach faces the open Atlantic, so waves roll in steadily and attract surfers, while a headland at one end makes a viewpoint over the coast.

Between roughly July and November the bay becomes a nursery for southern right whales, which come up from the cold Antarctic waters to give birth and raise their calves. You can often spot them from the beach or the headlands, blowing and slapping their tails, and the area around Imbituba has been officially called the national capital of the right whale. Patience, binoculars and a quiet morning are all you need, and it is hard to describe the feeling of watching a mother and calf only a few hundred metres offshore.

Riding in is a pleasure. From Florianópolis, you take the BR-101 south through flat coastal country, then turn toward the sea on smaller roads that wind among hills and eucalyptus and past small villages. Traffic thins quickly once you leave the highway, though sandy patches, dogs and cyclists make it worthwhile to go gently, and the final approach down to the beach is a narrow road lined with pousadas and cafés. Midweek in the off-season, the village is almost empty, while January is packed.

Praia do Rosa itself is small and has limited services, so fill the tank before arriving, in Imbituba, a town of over forty thousand, or in Garopaba just to the north. The village has surf shops, simple restaurants serving fresh fish and caipirinhas, and plenty of places to stay in every price range. The sun is strong, so bring sunscreen, and keep a light rain jacket, as sea fog and showers come in from the south. Sunset from the headland is hard to beat.
t.irkeshtam@39.7,74.0:
Irkeshtam is the end of the line, or the start of the next one. It is a border post high in the Alay mountains, where the road from Osh and Sary-Tash reaches the frontier with China and the long way down to Kashgar begins. The setting is bare and enormous: a wide, treeless valley at the foot of the Trans-Alay range, with lines of trucks, a few buildings and mountains that keep going until they turn to blue haze. It is not a place to linger, but it is the kind of place that makes you think about distance.

The ride from Sary-Tash is a quiet pleasure. The road follows the broad Alay valley eastward for some eighty kilometres or so, mostly paved though with sections of rough surface and frost heave, and the traffic is a mix of Chinese trucks, shared taxis and herders on horseback. To the south, the Trans-Alay range shines with snow, and on a clear day the high peaks of the Pamirs, including Peak Lenin, rise above the horizon. Light here is clean and hard, and the air is thin. Wind can be fierce, so expect a constant lean on the bike.

This corridor has served trade for ages, with camel trains carrying goods between Kashgar and the Fergana valley long before trucks took over. The border itself is a modern, bureaucratic place, and rules for foreign travellers and especially private vehicles change often. Crossing into China on your own motorcycle usually requires advance arrangements, permits and a guide, and hours are limited, with closures on holidays. Check the current situation well before you set out, because turning up on a hope is a fine way to waste a day.

There is no real town here, so supplies are a matter of planning. Fuel should be topped up in Sary-Tash or Osh, with a margin for the return. Small cafes and guesthouses near the border serve tea, noodles and bread, and a few yurt camps can be found in the valley during summer. Dress for cold, even in July; the altitude is around three thousand metres, nights are sharp, and weather can change in an hour. If you only come to look at the mountains and the border, you will still leave glad you did.
t.karakoram highway point 7@36.5,74.9:
Passu is a few houses and a great deal of mountain. Sharp, serrated peaks known as the Passu Cones rise straight above the village like a row of dark teeth, and the Passu Glacier slides down the valley beside the road to end close to the Hunza River, a tongue of ice scattered with grey rubble. This is Upper Hunza, locally called Gojal, and everything here is bigger, drier and colder than in the lower valley. The altitude is around 2,400 metres.

The highway passes the village on a high bench, with the river down in a wide gravelly bed. Riding this section is a joy: the surface is good in most years, the corners are long and open, and the views change every few minutes. Lake Attabad, created in 2010 when a huge landslide dammed the river upstream, drowned part of the old road, and the highway now passes through new tunnels built by Chinese engineers beside the lake. The colour of the water is a startling turquoise.

You can walk out to the Passu suspension bridges, a series of narrow wooden-planked crossings over the river that have become famous for their sketchy appearance. Watching others cross is plenty for most riders. Guesthouses in Passu are modest and friendly, serving local food such as walnut cake and apricot soup, and the village has good places to sit with tea while the sun slides across the cones. Fuel is not reliable in the village itself, so fill up in Aliabad or Gulmit if you can, and ask in Sost for the pump near the border.

Light is the main reason to stay. In the morning the cones glow orange, and by dusk they turn a deep blue. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, while summer gets warm during the day but stays cool at night. Winters are harsh and the highway can close.

Wind funnels through the valley most afternoons, so expect gusts. Wear layers, because a ride that begins in a warm shirt can end in a jacket and gloves. Glaciers shift, and rockfall happens along this stretch, so stop only in places that feel safe, and watch the slopes above.
t.serra do rio do rastro point 3@-28.3,-49:
At the top of the serra the road eases, the forest gives way to open grassland and araucaria pines, and the whole sky seems to widen. The viewpoint here looks back down over the escarpment, and on a clear morning you can watch cloud pour into the valleys beneath you like milk. The altitude is around 1,400 metres or more, and the temperature is noticeably cooler, with frost possible on winter nights.

Lauro Muller is about twenty-four kilometres behind, and the nearest large towns, such as Sao Joaquim on the plateau, are farther on. There is little here beyond a few kiosks and small stalls, and fuel is not available at the viewpoint, so plan ahead. The plateau towns have services, and the local specialities include hot pinhao, the nut of the araucaria, roasted in winter, along with sausages, cheese and good apples.

This part of Santa Catarina is the coldest in Brazil, and in some winters snow falls on the high ground, drawing crowds from the rest of the country who are rarely able to see it. The plateau, known as the Serra Catarinense, has a distinct culture of cattle ranching and farming, and the region is also gaining recognition for its wine, produced in cool vineyards at high altitude.

Riding along the plateau is a relaxed contrast to the climb. The road is wide, the curves are gentle, and the landscape is open, with long views over rolling hills. Wind can be sharp, and the weather changes quickly, with morning mist giving way to sun. On the way back down, take extra care, since heavy braking and cold tyres can be a poor mix. Late afternoon light on the escarpment is lovely, and a stop at the viewpoint to see the lights of the coast begin to twinkle is a fitting end to the day.
t.near aliabad@36.3,74.7:
Hunza is the valley that makes people fall in love with northern Pakistan. Here, around Aliabad and Karimabad, the Karakoram Highway runs along a terrace above the Hunza River, and the mountains are on a scale that is hard to take in: Rakaposhi, at more than 7,700 metres, rises almost straight up from the valley floor to the south, and the peaks of Ultar Sar and Ladyfinger tower over Karimabad to the north. Below them, the valley is a green oasis of terraced fields, poplars and apricot orchards, watered by ancient irrigation channels that bring glacial meltwater down from the mountains.

Karimabad, the main town, is perched on the slopes above the highway, and above it stands Baltit Fort, a fortress-palace of stone and wood that was the seat of the Mirs of Hunza for centuries. It was restored by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture and is now a museum, with superb views over the valley. A little lower down, the older Altit Fort sits on a cliff above the river, said to be around a thousand years old. Hunza was an independent princely state until the 1970s, and the Mir ruled from these forts. Most people here are Ismaili Muslims, followers of the Aga Khan, and the valley is known for its high literacy rates and for its long-lived people, although the stories of their longevity are probably exaggerated.

The riding here is the highlight of the KKH. The road is generally well surfaced after its reconstruction with Chinese help, and it follows the river through the valley with long, sweeping curves and dramatic views. North of Karimabad, the road passes the Attabad Lake, formed in 2010 when a huge landslide blocked the river, and then continues toward the Chinese border at the Khunjerab Pass. Landslides are a constant risk, especially in spring and after heavy rain, and the road can be closed for hours or days.

Aliabad has fuel, shops and simple restaurants, and Karimabad has plenty of guesthouses, hotels and cafes. Try the dried apricots, apricot oil and walnut cake, and the local buckwheat bread. In spring, from late March to April, the apricot and cherry trees blossom, and in autumn, in October, the poplars turn golden.
t.near lauro muller@-28.4,-49.5:
Lauro Müller is a coal-mining town at the foot of the Serra do Rio do Rastro, one of the most famous roads in Brazil, and it sits in a quiet, green valley under a wall of cliffs. The town of ten thousand has a modest, working look, with a railway that once carried coal to the coast and the faded colour of an industry that has declined. The name honours Lauro Müller, a Brazilian engineer and politician born in this region in the nineteenth century, who served as governor of the state and later as a government minister.

The mountain behind the town is the attraction. The Serra do Rio do Rastro is an escarpment where the high plateau of southern Brazil drops sharply toward the coast, and the road climbs it in a spectacular series of switchbacks, with about two hundred and eighty-four bends cut into the slope. The road rises roughly a thousand metres in a short distance, and from the viewpoint near the top you can see the whole serpentine ribbon below, with the coastal plain stretching to the sea in the distance. On clear days, the panorama takes your words away.

The bends are tight, and the surface is generally good, but traffic can be heavy with trucks that crawl up the slope, and tourists who stop for photographs. In the early morning, fog often fills the valley, and when the sun breaks through, the cloud sinks below the road like a white sea. Rain makes the surface slick, and in winter, temperatures at the top can fall close to freezing, with the occasional dusting of snow. Ride up in the morning for the best light and the least traffic.

Another remarkable road in the region is Corvo Branco, a road cut through the rock of the escarpment between walls that tower high above the vehicles, with a dramatic view out over the canyon. It is reached from the plateau side and is a popular excursion.

Lauro Müller has fuel stations, small shops, bakeries and simple restaurants, and nearby Orleans and Urussanga offer more choice. The local food includes sausage, polenta and wine, a legacy of Italian settlers who came to this part of Santa Catarina. The best time to ride is autumn and spring, with clear air and moderate temperatures.
